payload.description:
The package is annotated — 159 of 177 defs carry return types and 143 carry annotated params — but python/src/aspergillus/ contains no py.typed marker, so PEP 561 makes mypy treat the whole package as Any for anything that imports it.

Measured consequence in the exophial repo (/home/rix/code/git_puller/repos/exophial): --strict's disallow_subclassing_any blocks the ONE mechanism aspergillus's own rule docstrings prescribe for retargeting a rule (subclass + override class attributes, src/exophial/lint_rules/in_process_e2e.py:26 'class ExophialInProcessE2E(InProcessE2E)'). exophial carries a scoped [[tool.mypy.overrides]] with disallow_subclassing_any = false to work around it (pebble exo-125.1), and that override is one of only two remaining exceptions to its repo-wide no-Any bans.

Fix: add an empty py.typed to python/src/aspergillus/ and make the build include it as package data. Then exophial can delete its override.

Note the same situation exists for pip-audit (exo-7f4.5), but that one is genuinely third-party and out of this repo's control.
payload.title: aspergillus ships no py.typed, so every consumer sees it as Any

payload.description:
Source: exo-ed84 in the exophial repo's tracker (a type-migration campaign
tripped this: introducing a `View` type alias across Slack Block Kit view
builders in `src/exophial/listen/slack/blocks.py`).

Request: Run `uv run pre-commit run aspergillus-check-duplicates --all-files
--hook-stage manual` on exophial main at 6ee3cbaa, then on a branch whose only
diff to blocks.py replaces the return annotation
`tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], str]` with the alias `View` for several
functions and reformats with `uv run ruff format`.

Expected: A commit that changes only type annotations, leaving every function
body byte-identical, produces the same check-duplicates verdict as its
parent.

Actual: On main the hook prints "Passed". On the annotation-only commit it
exits 1, reporting 2 duplicate group(s) among 4 functions whose BODIES never
changed in the diff. `git diff` shows zero changed lines inside any of the
four function bodies.

Root cause (verified by direct execution against `duplicates.py`'s pure
functions, not by reading): `_hash_function` renders the type-2-normalized
FunctionDef via `module.code_for_node(normalized)` and hashes that TEXT. Two
things leak into this text that have nothing to do with body structure:

1. Parameter/return type annotations are NOT stripped by `_Normalizer` — only
   identifiers and literals are collapsed. Two functions with identical
   bodies but a short alias (`View`) vs. a long generic
   (`tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], str]`) hash differently purely from the
   annotation's own AST shape (Name vs. Subscript), even though annotations
   carry no runtime/logic content.
2. `code_for_node` renders using each node's OWN concrete whitespace
   metadata (leading blank lines, per-parameter trailing commas/newlines
   inside a wrapped signature). Reformatting a multi-line signature to a
   single line via `ruff format` — which is exactly what happens when a long
   annotation gets replaced by a short one — changes this rendered text even
   though nothing in `ast.parse` terms changed.

Repro (executed against the exact pinned v0.3.0 source at
`python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py`, no import of the installed package
needed):

    src_before = '''"""Module docstring."""

    from __future__ import annotations


    def ack_view(status: str) -> View:
        blocks = [{"type": "section", "text": status}]
        return blocks, "ack"


    def escalation_view(
        reason: str,
    ) -> tuple[list[dict[str, str]], str]:
        blocks = [{"type": "section", "text": reason}]
        return blocks, "escalation"
    '''

    src_after = '''"""Module docstring."""

    from __future__ import annotations


    def ack_view(status: str) -> View:
        blocks = [{"type": "section", "text": status}]
        return blocks, "ack"


    def escalation_view(reason: str) -> View:
        blocks = [{"type": "section", "text": reason}]
        return blocks, "escalation"
    '''

`find_duplicate_groups(extract_function_records(src_before, "x.py"), 1,
frozenset())` -> 0 groups. Same call on `src_after` -> 1 group
(`ack_view`, `escalation_view`) — a false positive: the diff between
`src_before` and `src_after` changes only `escalation_view`'s return
annotation and its consequent formatting; neither function's body changed.

Proposed and empirically validated fix (both parts needed; tested against
the repro above, both directions — genuinely-different-body functions stay
non-duplicate across an annotation-only edit, and functions whose bodies
were ALREADY identical report the identical verdict before and after):

1. In `_Normalizer`, strip annotations entirely rather than merely
   collapsing their identifiers:

       def leave_Param(self, original_node, updated_node):
           return updated_node.with_changes(annotation=None)

       def leave_FunctionDef(self, original_node, updated_node):
           return updated_node.with_changes(returns=None)

2. In `_hash_function`, canonicalize away layout/whitespace before hashing
   by round-tripping the normalized+annotation-stripped text through the
   stdlib `ast` module (which has no concept of blank lines, trailing
   commas, or signature wrapping):

       import ast
       ...
       def _hash_function(module, func):
           normalized = func.visit(_Normalizer())
           assert isinstance(normalized, cst.FunctionDef)
           code = module.code_for_node(normalized)
           canonical = ast.unparse(ast.parse(code))
           return hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

`ast.unparse` is safe post-normalization because `_Normalizer` has already
collapsed every string/f-string/literal to a fixed marker, so there is no
quote-style or f-string-vs-concat ambiguity left for it to introduce.

Impact: a landing can be blocked by a duplicate group that no body change
introduced — false-positive gate failures during any annotation/typing
migration. Reproducible: always. Severity: maintainability, low-blast-radius
(check-duplicates only), but directly blocked exo-ed84 in exophial.

Downstream: exophial pins `aspergillus==0.3.0` via
`[tool.uv.sources]` (git tag `v0.3.0`) — a fix here needs a new release tag
before exophial's pin can be bumped to pick it up; exo-ed84 is tracking that
dependency and is filed as blocked on this pebble.
payload.title: check-duplicates verdict changes when only a type annotation changes

payload.description:
Post-landing merged-tree handoff-corpus validation (exo-942.9.3) found handoff file(s) that do not validate against done.schema.json:

- .pebbles/handoffs/asp-047.yaml: verify_transcript: 'checks' is a required property; verify_transcript: Additional properties are not allowed ('change_assertion_a_wheel_external_install', 'change_assertion_b_git_tag_external_install', 'pre_commit', 'regression_gate_pytest' were unexpected)
- .pebbles/handoffs/asp-108.yaml: verify_transcript: 'checks' is a required property; <root>: 'cost' is a required property; verify_transcript: Additional properties are not allowed ('backtest_fixit_lint', 'pre_commit', 'python_pytest' were unexpected); <root>: {'status': 'completed', 'pebble_id': 'asp-108', 'branch': 'pebble/asp-r2', 'commits': ['15f3220529294d4a7ef3a8b42c78b4f21fe90a3a'], 'files_changed': ['aspergillus/python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py', 'aspergillus/python/src/aspergillus/io_blocklist.py'], 'tests_added': [], 'docs_updated': [], 'summary': 'io_blocklist pandas-rename false-positive fixed, on the SAME branch/commit as asp-594 (one round-trip).   What did you do? List the exact steps to reproduce, in order. Run aspergillus's check-duplicates against a codebase containing near-miss or semantic duplicates (type-3/type-4 clones): two functions that share a substantial copied spine — a verbatim-identical inner closure plus an identical call, and duplicated statement sequences — embedded in two structurally different functions. (Originally observed in exophial3 on src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py:drive vs src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py:put.)
  What did you expect to happen? check-duplicates flags (a) type-3 near-miss/gapped clones (copied fragments inside differently-shaped functions with added/removed/changed statements) and (b) type-4 semantic clones (functionally equivalent, syntactically different code) — or at minimum states in its own docs that its scope is type-2-only.
  What actually happened? Include the exact error text or output. The detector at python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py normalizes each function body (identifiers -> _ID, literals -> type markers; _Normalizer), renders the whole normalized body, sha256-hashes it (_hash_function), and groups only functions whose ENTIRE normalized body hashes identically (find_duplicate_groups). Fragment-level near-miss (type-3) and semantically-equivalent-but-syntactically-different (type-4) matches never produce a hit, on any input, by construction of the whole-body-hash comparison; a substantial duplicated spine embedded in two differently-shaped functions yields 'no duplicate functions found'. duplicates.py's own docstring self-declares 'This is what makes the hash a type-2 clone signature'.
  Which surface or component? (e.g. gateway route, mobile screen, CLI verb) aspergillus check-duplicates (python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py: _Normalizer, _hash_function, find_duplicate_groups)
  What environment and version? (OS, app/gateway build or commit, network) aspergillus repo, Python rule pack (python/)
  Is it reproducible? (always / intermittently / once) — and how often. always
  What is the impact / severity? Who is blocked and how badly? The duplication gate is scoped to type-2 (renamed whole-function) clones only. Type-3 near-miss/gapped clones and type-4 semantic clones pass the gate uncaught. Standard type-1..4 clone taxonomy (Roy & Cordy clone-detection survey; Bellon et al. clone-tool comparison).
  What activity was underway when this was found? (ODC Activity — e.g. testing, code review, normal usage, reproduction attempt) design review
  What condition or event exposed the defect? (ODC Trigger — e.g. a config change, concurrent access, a boundary/edge-case input, an unusual workload) design conformance
  Which quality/capability dimension does this affect? (ODC Impact — e.g. reliability, usability, capability, performance, security, maintainability, standards, requirements — distinct from the severity/who's-blocked question above) maintainability
  Decomposed child: Replace aspergillus's current type-2 clone detector in python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py — which normalizes identifiers to _ID and literals to type markers via _Normalizer, sha256-hashes the ENTIRE normalized function body via _hash_function, and groups only functions whose entire normalized body hashes identically via find_duplicate_groups — with a fragment-granular comparison. Keep the _Normalizer identifier->_ID / literal->type-marker normalization, but compare over SLIDING WINDOWS of normalized statement sequences instead of one whole-body hash, so a copied spine embedded inside a larger, differently-shaped function is caught. This fixes the defect where a copied spine — a verbatim-identical inner closure plus an identical call, plus duplicated statement sequences — embedded in two structurally different functions is missed today because the comparison hashes the entire normalized body (duplicates.py's own docstring self-declares the hash is 'a type-2 clone signature' over the whole body). Each detected type-2 pair must carry its clone type label and a similarity score, and boilerplate (trivial dunders/getters/pass-only bodies) must be excluded. Build a pytest suite including: fixtures from the Roy & Cordy (2007) editing-scenario taxonomy for type-2 edits, Bellon et al. (2007) reference clones, BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al. 2014) pairs labeled T2, and the regression fixture from the original report — two functions (originally observed in exophial3 as src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py:drive vs src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py:put) sharing a verbatim copied spine embedded in two structurally different bodies, which currently yields 'no duplicate functions found' and must now be flagged.

criticality: negligible

goal: Make aspergillus's duplicate detector catch a copied statement spine embedded inside two differently-shaped functions, label and score every reported pair, exclude boilerplate, and prove all of this with a pytest suite covering the drive/put regression and three named clone-research fixtures.

restatement:
  The duplicate-function detector in python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py hashes the whole normalized function body. Its function find_duplicate_groups groups two functions only when their whole-body hashes match exactly. This method misses a real defect class. A copied spine — an identical inner closure, an identical call, and a duplicated statement sequence — can sit inside two functions that differ elsewhere. The whole-body hashes then differ, so the tool reports no duplicate. The reported case is exophial3's function drive in src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py against exophial3's function put in src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py. These two functions share a verbatim copied spine inside two structurally different bodies. Today check-duplicates reports 'no duplicate functions found' for this pair. The fix keeps the _Normalizer's identifier-to-_ID and literal-to-type-marker normalization unchanged. The fix replaces the single whole-body hash with a sliding-window comparison over sequences of normalized statements. This sliding-window comparison catches a copied spine wherever it sits inside a function, not only when the spine is the whole function. Each reported type-2 clone pair must carry a clone-type label and a numeric similarity score. The detector must never report a boilerplate body as a duplicate. Boilerplate bodies are trivial dunder methods, simple getters, and pass-only bodies. This exclusion applies even when two boilerplate bodies match verbatim. The change ships with a pytest suite. The suite proves the general fragment-detection capability. The suite reproduces the drive/put regression. The suite proves boilerplate exclusion. The suite adds three further fixtures, each labeled for one clone-detection research source: the Roy & Cordy (2007) type-2 editing-scenario taxonomy, the Bellon et al. (2007) reference-clone benchmark, and the BigCloneBench corpus from Svajlenko et al. (2014). The detector must flag each of these three fixtures as a type-2 duplicate.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: The detector replaces the whole-body hash comparison with a sliding-window comparison over normalized statement sequences. This change lets it catch a copied spine embedded inside a larger, differently-shaped function.
- c2: The _Normalizer's identifier-to-_ID and literal-to-type-marker normalization stays exactly as it is today.
- c3: Every reported type-2 clone pair carries a clone-type label.
- c4: Every reported type-2 clone pair carries a numeric similarity score.
- c5: The detector excludes boilerplate bodies — trivial dunder methods, simple getters, and pass-only bodies — from duplicate reporting, even when two such bodies match verbatim.
- c6: The regression fixture — function drive from exophial3's src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py and function put from exophial3's src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py, sharing a verbatim copied spine inside two structurally different bodies — is now flagged as a duplicate pair, where it previously produced 'no duplicate functions found'.
- c7: The pytest suite includes a fixture labeled for the Roy & Cordy (2007) type-2 editing-scenario taxonomy, and the detector flags it as a duplicate.
- c8: The pytest suite includes a fixture labeled for the Bellon et al. (2007) reference-clone benchmark, and the detector flags it as a duplicate.
- c9: The pytest suite includes a fixture labeled for the BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al. 2014) type-2 (T2) clone category, and the detector flags it as a duplicate.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: A person runs the duplicate checker on two functions with different surrounding code but the same inner helper and the same duplicated block. The checker reports the two functions as a duplicate pair.
- c2: A person runs the normalizer on two functions that differ only in variable names and literal values. The normalizer still marks them as identical, exactly as it does today.
- c3: A person runs the duplicate checker on a known pair of duplicate functions. The reported pair carries a clone-type label.
- c4: A person runs the duplicate checker on a known pair of duplicate functions. The reported pair carries a similarity score above zero.
- c5: A person runs the duplicate checker on two files that share the same trivial pass-only __init__ method and the same one-line getter. The checker does not report them as duplicates.
- c6: A person runs the duplicate checker on the drive/put regression fixture. The checker reports drive and put as a duplicate pair, instead of the old 'no duplicate functions found' result.
- c7: A person runs the duplicate checker on the Roy & Cordy type-2 editing-scenario fixture. The checker reports its two functions as a duplicate pair.
- c8: A person runs the duplicate checker on the Bellon et al. reference-clone fixture. The checker reports its two functions as a duplicate pair.
- c9: A person runs the duplicate checker on the BigCloneBench T2 fixture. The checker reports its two functions as a duplicate pair.

restatement:
  The aspergillus package must import cleanly from its source tree when it is not installed as a distribution. The acceptance-probe contract in scripts/CLAUDE.md runs probes with the bare system python3, with no venv and only the standard library. Under that contract, `PYTHONPATH=python/src python3 -c 'import aspergillus'` currently fails with `importlib.metadata.PackageNotFoundError: No package metadata was found for aspergillus`. The cause is the unconditional `__version__ = version('aspergillus')` call at import time in python/src/aspergillus/__init__.py. The requirement is that this import succeeds, and that `aspergillus.__version__` resolves to a fallback string when no installed distribution metadata is present. Any stdlib-only probe that adds python/src to sys.path and imports the package must therefore work under bare python3. When the package is installed, the version must still come from the distribution metadata, so the single source of truth does not change. The source comment that says the lookup 'never falls back' is false, and it must not stay in the file.

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

  What did you do? List the exact steps to reproduce, in order. Run aspergillus's check-duplicates against a codebase containing near-miss or semantic duplicates (type-3/type-4 clones): two functions that share a substantial copied spine — a verbatim-identical inner closure plus an identical call, and duplicated statement sequences — embedded in two structurally different functions. (Originally observed in exophial3 on src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py:drive vs src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py:put.)
  What did you expect to happen? check-duplicates flags (a) type-3 near-miss/gapped clones (copied fragments inside differently-shaped functions with added/removed/changed statements) and (b) type-4 semantic clones (functionally equivalent, syntactically different code) — or at minimum states in its own docs that its scope is type-2-only.
  What actually happened? Include the exact error text or output. The detector at python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py normalizes each function body (identifiers -> _ID, literals -> type markers; _Normalizer), renders the whole normalized body, sha256-hashes it (_hash_function), and groups only functions whose ENTIRE normalized body hashes identically (find_duplicate_groups). Fragment-level near-miss (type-3) and semantically-equivalent-but-syntactically-different (type-4) matches never produce a hit, on any input, by construction of the whole-body-hash comparison; a substantial duplicated spine embedded in two differently-shaped functions yields 'no duplicate functions found'. duplicates.py's own docstring self-declares 'This is what makes the hash a type-2 clone signature'.

Default thresholds: dissimilarity <= 0.30 (i.e. >= 70% similar), AND a minimum clone size of >= 5 statements or >= 10 source lines to suppress coincidental matches. Both thresholds must be configurable. Report a type-3 pair only if it clears BOTH the similarity threshold and the minimum-size threshold; each report carries its clone type label and similarity score; boilerplate (trivial dunders/getters/pass-only bodies) is excluded. Build a pytest suite including: fixtures from the Roy & Cordy (2007) editing-scenario taxonomy for type-3 edits, Bellon et al. criticality: negligible

goal: Add configurable, near-miss (type-3) clone detection to aspergillus's check-duplicates, built on its existing type-2 normalization, with literature-grounded proof that it catches edited copies without false-flagging boilerplate.

restatement:
  The duplicate-function checker (python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py, run via `aspergillus check-duplicates`) currently only catches type-2 clones: two functions whose normalized forms hash IDENTICALLY (same code shape after identifiers become _ID and literals become type markers). It misses the common real-world case where someone copies a function and then edits it — adds a step, drops a step, changes a comparison — so the normalized forms no longer hash equal even though the functions are still mostly the same code. This request adds type-3 (near-miss / gapped) clone detection on top of that existing machinery: break each function into its normalized statement sequence, measure how similar two candidate functions' sequences are, and report a pair as a type-3 clone when they are similar enough (a configurable dissimilarity ceiling, default 0.30, meaning at least 70% similar) AND big enough (a configurable minimum size, default >= 5 statements or >= 10 source lines) to rule out coincidence. Each type-3 report must carry the label 'type-3' and a numeric similarity score between 0 and 1. Boilerplate — trivial dunder methods, one-line getters, pass-only bodies — must never be reported this way, even if two boilerplate bodies happen to look similar. The feature must be proven against known patterns from the clone-detection literature: a Roy & Cordy (2007) type-3 editing scenario (a copied fragment with statements added, removed, or changed) must be caught, while a pair edited past the similarity ceiling must not be; a BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al. 2014) ST3/MT3-style near-miss pair must be caught; and the specific regression that motivated this work — two functions with wildly different surrounding logic that nonetheless share one long, verbatim, untouched block of statements — must be caught as at least a type-3 clone, since today it is missed entirely. Type-4 (semantically-equivalent but textually dissimilar) clone detection is explicitly out of scope; that is separate work, asp-d88.4.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: Extend python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py to detect type-3 near-miss/gapped clones on top of the existing type-2 normalized-function-hash matching, reporting two functions as a type-3 clone when their normalized per-statement sequences are similar above a threshold but not identical.
- c2: Use a NiCad-style normalized-statement-sequence similarity technique with a default dissimilarity threshold of <= 0.30 (that is, similarity >= 70%), and make this threshold configurable.
- c3: Apply a minimum clone size gate of >= 5 statements OR >= 10 source lines, configurable, to suppress coincidental matches.
- c4: Report a type-3 pair only when it clears BOTH the similarity threshold and the minimum clone size threshold.
- c5: Each type-3 report carries the clone type label 'type-3' and a similarity score in the range (0, 1).
- c6: Exclude boilerplate -- trivial dunder methods, one-line getters, and pass-only bodies -- from type-3 clone candidacy.
- c7: A Roy & Cordy (2007) type-3 editing scenario -- a copied fragment with statements added, removed, or changed -- must be reported as a type-3 clone, and a pair whose edits push it below the similarity threshold must not be reported.
- c8: Detect a BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al. 2014) ST3/MT3-style near-miss clone pair as a type-3 clone.
- c9: Flag as at least a type-3 clone the regression case of two functions sharing a verbatim copied spine embedded in two structurally different bodies -- the case originally observed in exophial3 as src/e_new_model/shell/drive.py:drive versus src/e_new_model/shell/driver.py:put, which previously yielded 'no duplicate functions found'.
- c10: Type-4 semantic clone detection is out of scope for this change; that is tracked separately as asp-d88.4.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: Checking two functions that do almost the same work, where one has an extra step spliced into an otherwise identical sequence, shows the checker reporting them as a near-miss match, not as an exact duplicate.
- c2: Checking a pair of functions that are about 75% alike shows them reported at the checker's normal settings, but checking the same pair with a much stricter similarity requirement shows them no longer reported.
- c3: Checking a tiny pair of near-miss functions, well under both size floors, shows them not reported at the checker's normal settings, but relaxing the size settings shows the same pair now reported.
- c4: Checking a pair of functions that is big enough but only about 40% alike shows them not reported, while checking a separate pair that is both big enough and about 80% alike shows them reported.
- c5: Looking at a reported near-miss pair shows it labeled as a 'type-3' clone with a similarity score strictly between 0 and 1.
- c6: Checking two near-miss equality-comparison dunder methods -- boilerplate that is similar and long enough to otherwise qualify -- shows them not reported as a clone.
- c7: Checking a copied fragment with one statement added, one removed, and one changed shows it reported as a near-miss clone, while checking a second pair edited so heavily that under 70% of it still matches shows it not reported.
- c8: Checking a small utility function against a near-miss rewrite of it, built in the style of a published BigCloneBench near-miss example, shows the pair reported as a near-miss clone.
- c9: Checking two functions built with completely different surrounding logic, but sharing one long, unedited block of statements in the middle, shows the pair reported as a near-miss clone.
- c10: The duplicate checker's own source file states, in its documentation, that detecting semantically-equivalent-but-textually-different clones (type-4) is out of scope for this change and is tracked separately as asp-d88.4.

Because type-4 recall is inherently limited, report them as a DISTINCT LOWER-CONFIDENCE, NON-BLOCKING tier (clone type 'type-4-candidate'), separate from the type-2/type-3 tiers and never failing the gate on their own. (2) Technique = a deterministic normalized SEMANTIC FEATURE VECTOR per function computed with the existing LibCST parse (no PDG/external dep): e.g. multiset of called-callable names, multiset of operators, literal-type counts, and control-flow-construct counts; compare vectors with a similarity threshold and report candidate pairs above it. (3) Each candidate carries clone type 'type-4-candidate' and a similarity score in (0,1). NO BigCloneBench / Java fixtures. (5) Type-1/2/3 are out of scope (other children).

Report type-4 hits as a distinct LOWER-CONFIDENCE 'candidate' tier, separate from the type-1/2/3 tiers, and do not fail or block the gate solely on a type-4 candidate hit, since type-4 recall is inherently limited. Each report carries its clone type ('type-4-candidate') and a similarity score, and excludes boilerplate (trivial dunders/getters/pass-only bodies). Build a pytest suite including fixtures from the Roy & Cordy (2007) editing-scenario taxonomy for type-4 edits and BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al. 2014) pairs labeled T4, asserting the detector assigns the correct candidate tier to each labeled pair.

criticality: negligible

goal: Add a non-blocking type-4 semantic clone candidate tier to aspergillus's duplicate checker, built from a deterministic LibCST-derived feature vector, and prove it with in-repo Python fixtures.

restatement:
  Aspergillus's duplicate-code checker (python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py) today finds type-1, type-2, and type-3 clones: exact or near-exact code copies. This request adds a separate, new capability: finding type-4 clones, pairs of functions that do the same job but are written in completely different code. Because this kind of match is much harder to prove correct, every type-4 match must be reported as a 'candidate' in its own tier, lower-confidence than the existing tiers, and a type-4 candidate must never by itself make the duplicate-check gate fail. The detector must build its judgment from a fixed, repeatable set of numbers computed for each function from the code's existing LibCST parse tree: how many times each function or method is called, which operators appear, how many literals of each type appear, and how many control-flow blocks (if, for, while, and so on) appear. It must not use a program-dependence-graph library or any other new external dependency. Two functions are reported as a type-4 candidate pair when their numbers are similar enough to cross a fixed threshold, and each reported pair carries the label 'type-4-candidate' and a similarity score strictly between 0 and 1. To prove the detector works, the repository must contain a Python example pair that does the same job in two different ways (for example an iterative loop that adds up a list against a call to the built-in sum(), or an iterative factorial against a recursive factorial), and running the detector on that pair must report it as a type-4 candidate. The repository must also contain a pair of clearly unrelated functions, and running the detector on that pair must not report it as a type-4 candidate. All example fixtures are written in Python inside this repository; none may come from BigCloneBench or from Java source, because BigCloneBench is a Java-only corpus and this detector only understands Python. Finding type-1, type-2, and type-3 clones is unchanged by this work; those tiers keep behaving exactly as they do today.

- c1: The type-4-candidate tier must be reported separately from the type-2 and type-3 tiers, and a type-4-candidate finding must never by itself make the duplicate-check gate fail or block.
- c2: The comparison the detector uses to find type-4 candidates must be deterministic: computed from the existing LibCST parse of each function, it must give the same similarity score every time it runs on the same pair of functions.
- c3: The detector must not use a PDG (program-dependence-graph) library or any other new external dependency; it must be built only on the existing LibCST parse.
- c4: Each reported type-4 candidate must carry the clone type 'type-4-candidate' and a similarity score strictly between 0 and 1.
- c5: The repository must contain an in-repo Python fixture pair that is functionally equivalent but syntactically different, for example an iterative for-loop sum versus the built-in sum(), or an iterative factorial versus a recursive factorial, and running the detector on this pair must report it as a type-4 candidate.
- c6: The repository must contain a clearly-unrelated Python function pair, and running the detector on this pair must not report it as a type-4 candidate.
- c7: No BigCloneBench or Java-derived fixtures may be used; all fixtures used to prove this feature are authored in Python inside this repository.

- c7: None of the new type-4 example files or the checker's own source mention BigCloneBench or its Java corpus.

The bare method name `rename` in IO_METHOD_NAMES collides with pandas DataFrame.rename / Series.rename (pure in-memory transforms), mis-flagging them ASP205/206 and (post asp-da5) mis-classifying them imperative-shell for ASP202.

Approach (PRECISE, not wholesale-delete): added _is_pandas_rename() in rules/level2.py and gated the bare-`rename` match in _walk_for_io_calls on `not (method == "rename" and _is_pandas_rename(node))`. A `.rename` call is a pure pandas transform (NOT I/O) when EITHER it carries a pandas-rename keyword (columns/index/mapper/axis/inplace/level/errors/ copy) OR its receiver is a COMPUTED expression (not a Name / attribute chain — you cannot filesystem-rename an arithmetic / chained result).

Tradeoff: this PRESERVES instance-form pathlib `Path.rename(target)` detection (simple-name receiver, single positional, no pandas kwarg) rather than dropping `rename` from IO_METHOD_NAMES wholesale. Documented residual ambiguity: `s.rename("x")` on a simple Series NAME with a single positional is shape-identical to `p.rename(target)` and is left matching (conservative — a real rename is never silently dropped). No backtest reproducer site hits that residual.

VERIFIED against the live backtest reproducer (`cd backtest && .venv/bin/python -m fixit lint src`, editable aspergillus resolving to this worktree): ZERO `rename` I/O findings — _normalize_dune_df (df.rename@68), _compute_pair_z (.rename@269/272), _scan_one_pair (.rename@355) all cleared. The 2 GENUINE pathlib sites remain: fixture_loader read_text@16 and data_fetcher mkdir@99 (each ASP205 + ASP206). Added Valid fixtures (df.rename(columns=…) pure; computed- receiver Series.rename pure) and an Invalid fixture (Path.rename(target) stays I/O) to ASP205. Full detail in handoffs/asp-594.yaml. Guiding principle honoured throughout: the min=2 assertion floor (NASA Rule #5) is NEVER lowered — the PREDICATE is made correct so genuinely-correct code is recognized/exempt BY CONSTRUCTION, not forced into theatre assertions.

── asp-594 (TS ASP202, parity with Python LowAssertionDensity) ── Three options-driven recognitions added to typescript/rules/asp202-min-assertions.js, each with a sensible default, matching the rule's existing options style:
(1) exemptMethods (default [constructor, toString, valueOf]) — parity with the Python sibling's EXEMPT_PREFIXES (__init__/__repr__/…). A constructor initialises fields; toString/valueOf are coercion hooks; none is a precondition-bearing shell function. Exemption is checked BEFORE the length gate (detected via node.parent MethodDefinition/ Property key, with kind==='constructor' handled).
(2) countErrReturns (default true) + errorResultCallees (default [err, errAsync]) — a `return err(...)` (neverthrow) counts as a precondition guard. In a codebase where eslint-plugin-functional BANS throw, the err-return IS the idiomatic precondition-failure: the moral equivalent of the Python sibling's raise-guard (COUNT_RAISE default on).
(3) recognizeUntrustedDischarge (default true) + resultCallees (default [ok, err, okAsync, errAsync]) — the load-bearing predicate refinement. A PURE function (no I/O) whose ONLY imperative-shell signal is an untrusted (any/unknown) parameter is treated as FUNCTIONAL CORE (exempt) when it DISCHARGES that input by construction, detected by two shapes in bodyDischarges(): (a) it returns a neverthrow Result (return ok(...) / return err(...)), so the unknown becomes a statically-typed Result<T,E> whose error arm is explicit (the parse-don't-validate boundary); or (b) it narrows a value with `instanceof`, after which tsc(strict) guarantees type-safe use in the matched branch and FORBIDS unguarded use of the still-unknown value in the others — so a pure unknown→union normalizer is safe in every branch by construction. This is a predicate change, NOT a count change: min stays >=2 and is simply inapplicable to the functional core (exactly like every other pure FC function the rule already exempts). A blind-coerce consumer of untrusted data (String(x) / Object.keys(x) with no guard) is NOT discharged and stays shell — the pre-existing INVALID fixtures (normalize: any→string, decode: unknown→ number) still flag, pinning that the discharge does not over-exempt.

THE 4 NAMED TS RESIDUALS, re-run with treatAwaitAsIo=false: - mobile/src/contracts/decode.ts :: decode(data: unknown) — RESOLVED by
  construction. Pure ajv-validate→neverthrow-Result adapter; returns
  ok/err → untrusted-discharge → functional core → exempt.
- mobile/src/errors/AppError.ts :: toAppError(e: unknown) — RESOLVED by
  construction. Pure total normalizer; narrows via `e instanceof Error`
  + exhaustive branches + unknownError fallback → instanceof-discharge →
  functional core → exempt.
- mobile/src/services/notifee-signals.ts :: FirebaseMessagingError
  constructor — RESOLVED. Constructor exemption (exemptMethods default).
- arcade/.../lib/x402.ts :: makeSessionRequiredFetch / fetchOrRefuse —
  INSPECTED. The OUTER makeSessionRequiredFetch only CLOSES OVER fetch
  (returns the wrapper, does no I/O at its own scope) and is ALREADY
  correctly exempt — the rule's existing skip-nested walk does not see
  the nested arrow's I/O, so no closed-over-I/O refinement was needed.
  The flagged function is the INNER `fetchOrRefuse` arrow, which
  GENUINELY calls `fetch` at its own scope (real imperative-shell I/O)
  and has exactly ONE precondition guard (the 402 → throw). This is a
  GENUINE min-2 case: it needs a real second assertion (e.g. an explicit
  check on `input`/`response`) added IN arcade — NOT a rule change. Per
  task instruction the rule was NOT hacked to silence it; reported here.


── asp-108 (Python io_blocklist pandas-rename false-positive) ── The bare method name `rename` in IO_METHOD_NAMES collides with pandas DataFrame.rename / Series.rename (pure in-memory transforms). Approach (precise, not wholesale-delete): added _is_pandas_rename() in rules/level2.py and gated the bare-`rename` match in _walk_for_io_calls on `not (method == "rename" and _is_pandas_rename(node))`. A `.rename` call is treated as a pure pandas transform (NOT I/O) when EITHER it carries a pandas-rename keyword (columns/index/mapper/axis/inplace/ level/errors/copy) OR its receiver is a COMPUTED expression (not a Name or attribute chain — you cannot filesystem-rename the result of an arithmetic / chained expression). payload.description:
Request:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust workspace that adopts Aspergillus gets every ASP rule checked mechanically on commit, the same way Python and TypeScript consumers do, including two whole-workspace checks: the same function body defined twice, and the same concept declared as a type in more than one crate.
Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus (first consumer: lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates), and the exophial workers committing into them.
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. A consumer copies or depends on aspergillus/rust (as it does today for rust/configs/clippy.toml) and runs the Rust rules over its workspace; each finding prints as `path:line: ASPnnn` and a finding in a blocking rule fails the run. docs/design.md's Rust column names, for every rule of Levels 2 and 3 and every ASP4xx rule that applies to Rust, the enforcing check: a clippy lint, a declarative ast-grep YAML rule under rust/ast-grep-rules/ (the engine TypeScript already uses under typescript/ast-grep-rules/), or a whole-workspace check; a rule the Rust language already enforces names the language feature, and a rule that does not apply to Rust says why. No entry reads 'Manual', 'planned' or 'Module structure'. A duplicate-function check reports two Rust functions whose normalized bodies are identical, as `aspergillus check-duplicates` does for Python. A duplicate-type check reports a struct or enum declared in one crate whose concept a type in another crate of the same workspace already declares, with an allowlist for intended cases.
What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Run against lobaria integrated a027fb9, the duplicate-type check reports the three declarations of Nanos (statechart/src/units.rs, pump-strategy/src/units.rs, hold-time-curve/src/input.rs) and of Receipt (statechart/src/edge.rs, pump-strategy/src/units.rs, hold-time-curve/src/input.rs) as findings. The ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 and ASP206 Rust checks each report a finding on a committed Rust fixture that violates the rule and none on a committed fixture that satisfies it, for every rule that has a Rust check. docs/design.md's Rust column has no 'Manual', 'planned' or 'Module structure' entry. A Rust consumer runs the checks with cargo and the ast-grep crates (ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config, ast-grep-language), with no Python or Node runtime in its gate path.
What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not a change to the Python or TypeScript rules. Not autofix: report-only, as the other languages are. Not a dylint compiler plugin as the required engine: ast-grep YAML plus the ast-grep crates is the engine lobaria already runs (lobaria chart/src/ast_grep_gate.rs, lob-979). The duplicate-type check does not flag two types that share only a name when their shapes differ (lobaria's per-module Refused, Carried, Hit and Finding types are distinct types with local meaning).
Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) aspergillus docs/design.md sections 'Level 2', 'Level 3', 'Catalog rules ASP4xx', 'Whole-project CLI tools' (check-duplicates, asp-21d); typescript/ast-grep-rules/*.yml; lobaria chart/src/ast_grep_gate.rs and scripts/gates/core-types-rules/*.yml (ast-grep YAML rules run on ast-grep-core/config/language 0.40.0 from Rust); lobaria integrated a027fb9: 454 pub type declarations carry 384 distinct names, 45 names declared more than once.
What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
Points: 13

restatement:
  Aspergillus today reports duplicate Python functions with `aspergillus check-duplicates`. This request asks for the same service for Rust. A new check reads a whole Cargo workspace. It reads every crate in that workspace, not one crate only. It normalizes each Rust function body the same way the Python detector normalizes a Python function body. It then reports each pair of functions whose normalized bodies are identical. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates, so a duplicate pair that sits in two different crates must still appear in the report.
  The check reports only. It never rewrites a scanned file. It prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. It prints nothing when the workspace holds no duplicate pair.
  The check is a Rust program. It builds and runs with cargo. It uses the ast-grep crates ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config and ast-grep-language to parse the Rust code. The consumer runs it in a gate that has no Python runtime and no Node runtime, so the check must produce its findings when python3 and node are absent.
  This work adds a new surface. It does not change the existing Python rules and it does not change the existing TypeScript rules. The Python duplicate detector keeps its present behaviour. Reference: aspergillus docs/design.md section 'Whole-project CLI tools' (check-duplicates, asp-21d).

restatement_clauses:
- C1: The check reads a whole Cargo workspace and reports a duplicate function pair whose two functions sit in two different crates of that workspace (the first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates).
- C2: The check reports two Rust functions whose normalized bodies are identical, the same way `aspergillus check-duplicates` reports duplicate Python functions today.
- C3: The check reports no finding when no two Rust functions in the scanned workspace have identical normalized bodies.
- C4: Each finding prints as `path:line: ASPnnn`.
- C5: The check reports only. It does not autofix, and it leaves every scanned file byte-identical.
- C6: The check builds and runs with cargo, and it uses the ast-grep crates ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config and ast-grep-language.
- C7: No Python runtime and no Node runtime is in the consumer gate path: the check prints its findings when python3 and node are not available.
- C8: This deliverable does not change the Python rules: `aspergillus check-duplicates` still reports duplicate Python functions.
- C9: This deliverable does not change the TypeScript rules: the TypeScript rule files keep their rule declarations.

acceptance_criteria:
- C1: A throwaway Cargo workspace holds two crates. Each crate holds one copy of the same function. The report names both crates.
- C2: A Rust file holds two functions with the same body shape but different function names, different variable names and different literal values. The check reports them as one duplicate pair.
- C3: A Cargo workspace holds only functions with different bodies. The check reports nothing.
- C4: The check runs on a workspace with a known duplicate pair. Every printed finding line reads as a file path, a colon, a line number, a colon, a space, and an ASP code with three digits. The count of lines that do not read that way is reported.
- C5: Every file of a workspace with a known duplicate pair is fingerprinted before the check runs and after it runs. The count of files whose content changed is reported together with the count of findings.
- C6: Cargo builds the check from the repository. The build result and the number of the three named ast-grep libraries (ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config, ast-grep-language) present in the build's library list are reported.
- C7: The check runs with `python`, `python3`, `node` and `npm` replaced by stand-ins that fail and record each call. The check still reports the known duplicate pair, and the number of recorded calls to those stand-ins is reported.
- C8: The existing Python duplicate report runs on a Python file that holds two copies of one function. It still names that duplicate group.
- C9: Each of the six TypeScript shape-rewrite rule files still carries its rule name line, and the ASP202 rule file still names ASP202.

restatement:

  The deliverable is a runnable Rust gate that lives under `aspergillus/rust`. A consumer adopts it the same way it adopts `rust/configs/clippy.toml` today: it copies the directory, or it declares a Cargo dependency on it. The gate evaluates those YAML rules from Rust, through the ast-grep crates `ast-grep-core`, `ast-grep-config` and `ast-grep-language`. A finding that comes from a rule marked blocking makes the whole run fail with a non-zero exit status. A workspace with nothing to report passes with a zero exit status, so the gate is usable as a commit or CI gate.

Everything the consumer executes to get a verdict is cargo and Rust crates. If `python`, `python3`, `node`, `npm` and `npx` are all absent from the machine, the gate still runs and still reports findings.

restatement:

restatement:
  Today aspergillus gives a Rust consumer only static configuration files (rust/configs/clippy.toml and rust/configs/cargo-lints.toml). Rust support is placeholder-tier: there is no runnable check. This work adds a working check runner for Rust. The runner is a Cargo crate at rust/ast-grep-gate/. A consumer copies it, or depends on it, the same way it uses rust/configs/clippy.toml today. The runner reads its checks from declarative ast-grep YAML rule files under rust/ast-grep-rules/. This is the same rule format and the same engine the TypeScript side uses under typescript/ast-grep-rules/. The runner drives the ast-grep crates from Rust: ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config and ast-grep-language. lobaria's chart/src/ast_grep_gate.rs and lobaria's scripts/gates/core-types-rules/*.yml are the prior art, and lobaria runs those three crates at version 0.40.0. A dylint compiler plugin is explicitly not the engine. One run covers every crate of a whole Cargo workspace. The runner prints one line per finding, in the exact form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The runner owns the closed set of severity values. It publishes that set, and it says which values in the set block. A finding from a blocking rule makes the run fail with a non-zero exit status. A run with no blocking finding succeeds. The runner never edits a source file: it reports only, exactly as the Python checks and the TypeScript checks do. Nothing in the run needs a Python runtime or a Node runtime; cargo plus the ast-grep crates are the whole toolchain. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates. The existing Python rules and the existing TypeScript rules stay exactly as they are.

- c3: A consumer builds the runner with cargo alone and then runs the built binary.
- c4: The runner takes its checks from the declarative ast-grep YAML rule files under rust/ast-grep-rules/: adding a rule file there adds its finding, and removing that rule file removes its finding.
- c5: One run of the runner over a Cargo workspace covers every member crate of that workspace.
- c6: The runner prints each finding on one line, in the exact form `path:line: ASPnnn`.
- c7: A finding from a rule whose severity is a blocking value makes the run exit non-zero. A run whose findings are all non-blocking exits 0, and a run with no finding exits 0.
- c8: The runner defines a closed set of severity values. It prints that complete set, and marks which values block, when a consumer runs it with `--severities`. It refuses a rule whose severity value is outside the set, and it names the bad value.
- c9: The runner reports only and never autofixes: no file in the checked workspace changes during a run.
- c10: No Python runtime and no Node runtime is in the gate path: the runner still reports findings when python3, python, node and npx are absent from PATH.
- c11: This work does not change the TypeScript rules: every rule file under typescript/ast-grep-rules/ keeps its `id:` declaration.
- c12: This work does not change the Python rules: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py and python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py both still carry their ASP rule identifiers.

The work publishes one coverage manifest at rust/rule-coverage.md. The manifest gives each rule in scope one enforcement mechanism label. The label set is closed and holds five values: clippy lint, ast-grep YAML rule, whole-workspace check, language feature, and not applicable. Other parts of this epic read this label set, so this part owns it. A rule that a real check enforces carries one of the first three labels. A rule that the Rust language already enforces carries the label "language feature" and names that feature. A rule that does not apply to Rust carries the label "not applicable" and states the reason. Each Rust check reports a finding and edits no source file, exactly as the Python checks and the TypeScript checks do. Each rule that has a Rust check carries two committed Rust fixtures. One fixture violates the rule, and the check reports a finding on it. The other fixture satisfies the rule, and the check reports no finding on it. ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 and ASP206 must each pass that fixture pair. The declarative rules are ast-grep YAML files under rust/ast-grep-rules/. They use the same ast-grep engine and the same YAML schema that typescript/ast-grep-rules/ uses. A dylint compiler plugin is not the engine, so the Rust README must stop naming dylint as the plan. The lobaria file set scripts/gates/core-types-rules/*.yml is the prior art. lobaria is the first consumer, and it is a Cargo workspace of 33 crates. goal: Add a Rust duplicate-function check to aspergillus that reports pairs of Rust functions with identical normalized bodies across a whole Cargo workspace, builds and runs with cargo and the ast-grep crates, prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`, and changes no Python or TypeScript rule.

restatement:
  Aspergillus today reports duplicate Python functions with `aspergillus check-duplicates`. This request asks for the same service for Rust. A new check reads a whole Cargo workspace. It reads every crate of that workspace, not one crate only. It normalizes each Rust function body the same way the Python detector normalizes a Python function body. It then reports each pair of functions whose normalized bodies are identical. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates. A duplicate pair that sits in two different crates must therefore appear in the report.
  "The same way as Python" has one exact meaning here, and the Python detector defines it. `python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py` collapses every variable-position identifier to one placeholder. It keeps every distinguishing token exact: the literal values, the called-function names, and the attribute names. Two functions that differ only in their names therefore match. Two functions that differ in a literal value therefore do not match. The Rust check adopts this same equivalence. The derived acceptance note that asks for a match across different literal values contradicts the Python reference the request itself names, so the Python reference governs.
  The check reports only. It never rewrites a scanned file. It prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. It prints no finding when the workspace holds no duplicate pair.
  The check is a Rust program. It builds and runs with cargo. It uses the ast-grep crates ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config and ast-grep-language to parse the Rust code. The consumer runs it in a gate that holds no Python runtime and no Node runtime. The check must therefore produce its findings when python3 and node are absent.
  This work adds a new surface. It does not change the existing Python rules. It does not change the existing TypeScript rules. The Python duplicate detector keeps its present behaviour. Reference: aspergillus docs/design.md section 'Whole-project CLI tools' (check-duplicates, asp-21d).

restatement_clauses:
- C1: The check reads a whole Cargo workspace. It reports a duplicate function pair whose two functions sit in two different crates of that workspace. The first consumer is lobaria, a Cargo workspace of 33 crates.
- C2: The check reports two Rust functions whose normalized bodies are identical, with the equivalence `aspergillus check-duplicates` uses for Python today: every variable-position identifier collapses to one placeholder, and the literal values stay exact. Two functions that differ only in their function name and their variable names are one duplicate pair. Two functions that differ in a literal value are not a duplicate pair.
- C3: The check reports no finding when no two Rust functions of the scanned workspace have identical normalized bodies.
- C4: Each finding prints as `path:line: ASPnnn`: a file path, a colon, a line number, a colon, a space, and an ASP code of three digits.
- C5: The check reports only. It does not autofix. It leaves every scanned file byte-identical.
- C6: The check builds and runs with cargo. It uses the three ast-grep crates ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config and ast-grep-language.
- C7: No Python runtime and no Node runtime is in the consumer gate path. The check prints its findings when python3 and node are not available.
- C8: This deliverable does not change the Python rules. `aspergillus check-duplicates` still reports duplicate Python functions.
- C9: This deliverable does not change the TypeScript rules. The six TypeScript shape-rewrite rule files keep their rule name lines, and the ASP202 rule file still names ASP202.

acceptance_criteria:
- C1: Build a throwaway Cargo workspace of two crates. Put one copy of the same function in each crate. Run the new check over the workspace. The report names a duplicate pair, and it names both crates.
- C2: Put two functions with the same body shape, different function names and different variable names in one Rust file. Put two more functions that are the same except for one number in a second Rust file. The check reports the first two as one duplicate pair. It reports no pair for the second two.
- C3: Build a Cargo workspace whose functions all have different bodies. Run the check over it. The check reports nothing.
- C4: Run the check on a workspace that holds a known duplicate pair. Read every printed finding line. Count the lines that do not read as a file path, a colon, a line number, a colon, a space, and an ASP code of three digits.
- C5: Fingerprint every file of a workspace that holds a known duplicate pair. Run the check. Fingerprint every file again. Count the files whose content changed, and count the findings.
- C6: Build the check from this repository with cargo. Report whether the build succeeded. Count how many of the three named ast-grep libraries (ast-grep-core, ast-grep-config, ast-grep-language) the build's library list holds.
- C7: Replace `python`, `python3`, `node` and `npm` with stand-ins that fail and that record each call. Run the check on a workspace that holds a known duplicate pair. The check still reports that pair, and the stand-ins record no call.
- C8: Run the existing Python duplicate report on a Python file that holds two copies of one function. It still names that duplicate group.
- C9: Each of the six TypeScript shape-rewrite rule files still carries its rule name line, and the ASP202 rule file still names ASP202.

A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. Reducer gate had failed 3/12 on the worker's uncommitted-capture 8d37be0 due to hermetic-env cargo/bun PATH + string-anchored ^rule: grep; husband fixed on the worker branch, validated all 12 acceptance oracles green in a faithful reproduction of the grading env, and verified integrated rust/ == validated tree.

husband-note (Rust gate env + engine): (1) HERMETIC GATE ENV — aspergillus grades every behavior oracle in a child env whose PATH is only uv/git/bash + system dirs and whose HOME is a fresh scratch dir, so cargo/rustc/bun are NOT reachable by name. Any oracle script that runs cargo or bun MUST prepend: export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" (the husband exposes real ~/.cargo/.rustup/.bun into scratch HOME via EXOPHIAL_ORACLE_DATA_DIRS on the reducer). (2) The .1 runner crate is already on the integration branch at rust/ — invoke it with: cargo run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --offline -- <workspace-dir>; findings print as path:line: ASPnnn, blocking finding -> non-zero exit. (3) The gate grep oracles are whole-file, NON-multiline: a structural grep like ^rule: or ^id: only matches a file that STARTS with that key. Keep every rust/ast-grep-rules/*.yml starting with the rule: mapping as line 1.

Post-landing merged-tree handoff-corpus validation (exo-942.9.3) found handoff file(s) that do not validate against done.schema.json:

- .pebbles/handoffs/asp-047.yaml: verify_transcript: 'checks' is a required property; verify_transcript: Additional properties are not allowed ('change_assertion_a_wheel_external_install', 'change_assertion_b_git_tag_external_install', 'pre_commit', 'regression_gate_pytest' were unexpected)
- .pebbles/handoffs/asp-108.yaml: verify_transcript: 'checks' is a required property; <root>: 'cost' is a required property; verify_transcript: Additional properties are not allowed ('backtest_fixit_lint', 'pre_commit', 'python_pytest' were unexpected); <root>: {'status': 'completed', 'pebble_id': 'asp-108', 'branch': 'pebble/asp-r2', 'commits': ['15f3220529294d4a7ef3a8b42c78b4f21fe90a3a'], 'files_changed': ['aspergillus/python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py', 'aspergillus/python/src/aspergillus/io_blocklist.py'], 'tests_added': [], 'docs_updated': [], 'summary': 'io_blocklist pandas-rename false-positive fixed, on the SAME branch/commit as asp-594 (one round-trip). The bare method name `rename` in IO_METHOD_NAMES collides with pandas DataFrame.rename / Series.rename (pure in-memory transforms), mis-flagging them ASP205/206 and (post asp-da5) mis-classifying them imperative-shell for ASP202.

Approach (PRECISE, not wholesale-delete): added _is_pandas_rename() in rules/level2.py and gated the bare-`rename` match in _walk_for_io_calls on `not (method == "rename" and _is_pandas_rename(node))`. payload.description:
Request:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer can exclude path globs from the aspergillus Rust checks so intentionally rule-violating fixture subtrees produce no findings, while genuine duplicates outside those paths still report.
Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting aspergillus (first consumer: lobaria), whose commit gate must report only genuine findings and skip the fixture inputs of their own gates.
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. Each of the three Rust check binaries — aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check, aspergillus-rust-dup-check and aspergillus-rust-gate — accepts a repeatable --exclude <glob> flag; a source file whose workspace-relative path matches any --exclude glob is not scanned and yields no finding. Run aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check over the lobaria workspace with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**': the printed findings name the five production duplicate concepts Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run, no printed line has a path under scripts/oracles/fixtures/, and no line reports statechart/src/chart.rs Owed or Hole (whose only other declarations were the excluded fixtures). Without the flag those excluded-path findings and the Owed and Hole findings are present.
What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Over a committed two-crate Rust fixture where one duplicated type is declared once under an excluded glob and once outside it, each of the three binaries prints the finding at the unexcluded path and omits the finding at the excluded path. Over the lobaria workspace with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**', aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check prints findings for exactly Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run and no path under scripts/oracles/fixtures/ and no Owed or Hole finding. Passing --exclude more than once excludes the union of the globs.
What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not a change to which types or functions count as duplicates — only which paths are scanned. The existing --allowlist by type name stays and coexists. Not autofix. No change to the Python or TypeScript checks.
Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) Same class of path-skip the workspace walker already does for target/ and hidden dirs; fnmatch/gitignore-style glob. Consumer case: lobaria scripts/oracles/fixtures/** are intentional rule-violating inputs to its chart-conformance and totality gates.
What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
Points: 3

Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting aspergillus (first consumer: lobaria), whose commit gate must report only genuine findings and skip the fixture inputs of their own gates.
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. Each of the three Rust check binaries — aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check, aspergillus-rust-dup-check and aspergillus-rust-gate — accepts a repeatable --exclude <glob> flag; a source file whose workspace-relative path matches any --exclude glob is not scanned and yields no finding. Run aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check over the lobaria workspace with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**': the printed findings name the five production duplicate concepts Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run, no printed line has a path under scripts/oracles/fixtures/, and no line reports statechart/src/chart.rs Owed or Hole (whose only other declarations were the excluded fixtures). Without the flag those excluded-path findings and the Owed and Hole findings are present.
What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Over a committed two-crate Rust fixture where one duplicated type is declared once under an excluded glob and once outside it, each of the three binaries prints the finding at the unexcluded path and omits the finding at the excluded path. Over the lobaria workspace with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**', aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check prints findings for exactly Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run and no path under scripts/oracles/fixtures/ and no Owed or Hole finding. Passing --exclude more than once excludes the union of the globs.
What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not a change to which types or functions count as duplicates — only which paths are scanned. The existing --allowlist by type name stays and coexists. Not autofix. No change to the Python or TypeScript checks.
Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) Same class of path-skip the workspace walker already does for target/ and hidden dirs; fnmatch/gitignore-style glob. Consumer case: lobaria scripts/oracles/fixtures/** are intentional rule-violating inputs to its chart-conformance and totality gates.
What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1"

criticality: negligible

goal: Give the three aspergillus Rust check binaries a repeatable --exclude <glob> flag that skips matching workspace-relative paths, so fixture subtrees produce no findings while duplicates outside those paths still report.

restatement:
  Today the three aspergillus Rust check binaries scan every source file of a Cargo workspace. A consumer cannot tell them to skip a subtree. That hurts a consumer whose own gates keep intentionally rule-violating inputs in the tree. The first such consumer is lobaria. Its scripts/oracles/fixtures/ subtree holds deliberate rule violations, and they feed lobaria's chart-conformance gate and totality gate. The Rust checks report those deliberate violations as findings. The findings are noise, and they hide the genuine findings.
  This work adds one path filter to the three Rust check binaries: aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check, aspergillus-rust-dup-check and aspergillus-rust-gate. Each binary accepts a --exclude flag that takes one glob. A consumer repeats the flag. Two or more flags exclude the union of their globs. The binary matches each glob against the workspace-relative path of a source file. The binary does not scan a file whose path matches. A file the binary does not scan produces no finding.
  The filter is the same class of path skip the workspace walker already does for target/ and for hidden directories. The glob syntax is the fnmatch or gitignore style a person expects, so scripts/oracles/fixtures/** names a whole subtree.
  The consumer demonstration is lobaria. A person runs aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check over the lobaria workspace with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**'. The printed findings name the five production duplicate concepts: Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run. No printed line carries a path under scripts/oracles/fixtures/. No line reports statechart/src/chart.rs Owed, and no line reports statechart/src/chart.rs Hole, because the only other declaration of each of those two concepts sat under the excluded fixtures path. The same run without the flag prints the excluded-path findings, and prints the Owed finding and the Hole finding.
  The flag changes only which paths a binary scans. It does not change which types or which functions count as duplicates. A file the binary still scans produces exactly the findings it produced before. The existing --allowlist flag, which suppresses a finding by type name, stays. A person uses both flags in one run, and each one does its own job. No binary edits a file: the checks stay report-only, with no autofix. The Python checks and the TypeScript checks get no exclusion flag and no other change.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: Each of the three Rust check binaries — aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check, aspergillus-rust-dup-check and aspergillus-rust-gate — accepts a repeatable --exclude <glob> flag and runs to completion when a person passes it.
- c2: Over a committed two-crate Rust fixture where one duplicated type is declared once under a path matching an --exclude glob and once outside it, each of the three binaries prints the finding at the unexcluded path and prints no finding at the excluded path.
- c3: Passing --exclude more than once excludes the union of the globs: no finding carries a path matching either glob, and a finding outside both globs still prints.
- c4: Over a committed workspace fixture that reproduces the lobaria layout, aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check run with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' prints findings naming exactly the five concepts Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run, prints no line whose path is under scripts/oracles/fixtures/, and prints no line reporting statechart/src/chart.rs Owed or statechart/src/chart.rs Hole.
- c5: Over that same lobaria-shaped fixture, and with no --exclude flag, aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check prints findings whose paths are under scripts/oracles/fixtures/, and prints the statechart/src/chart.rs Owed finding and the statechart/src/chart.rs Hole finding.
- c6: The existing --allowlist flag, which suppresses a finding by type name, stays and coexists with --exclude: one run that passes both prints no finding naming the allowlisted type, prints no finding whose path matches the excluded glob, and still prints the remaining findings.
- c7: The --exclude flag changes only which paths a binary scans, never which types or functions count as duplicates: the findings of a run with an --exclude glob are exactly the findings of the same run without it, minus the findings whose path matches that glob.
- c8: The binaries stay report-only with no autofix: no file of the checked workspace changes during a run that uses --exclude.
- c9: This work does not change the Python checks or the TypeScript checks: python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py, python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py, python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py and the rule files under typescript/ast-grep-rules/ declare no --exclude option.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: A person starts each of the three Rust checkers in turn and gives each one two path patterns to skip, one pattern per flag. Each of the three programs accepts the patterns and finishes its run.
- c2: A person checks a small two-part Rust project in which the same concept is declared twice: once inside the folder they asked to skip, and once outside it. Each of the three checkers reports the declaration outside the skipped folder, and reports nothing inside it.
- c3: A person names two different folders to skip, one per flag, in a single run. The report holds nothing from either folder, and still holds a finding from a third place that the person did not skip.
- c4: A person checks a stored copy of the lobaria project layout with the duplicate-type checker, and asks it to skip everything under scripts/oracles/fixtures/. The report holds five findings, and they name Bps, SignedLamports, TrajectoryRow, Cut and Run. No line points at a file under scripts/oracles/fixtures/. No line reports Owed or Hole in statechart/src/chart.rs.
- c5: A person checks the same stored copy of the lobaria project layout, and asks for no folder to be skipped. The report now holds lines that point at files under scripts/oracles/fixtures/, and it holds the Owed finding and the Hole finding.
- c6: In one run a person names a type to let through by name, and separately names a folder to skip. The report holds no line for that type name, holds no line from that folder, and still holds the other findings.
- c7: A person checks the same project twice: once with a folder skipped, once with nothing skipped. The second report equals the first report plus exactly the lines that point into the skipped folder, and nothing else differs.
- c8: A person records the exact content of every file of a project, runs a checker over it with a folder skipped, and compares the files afterwards. Nothing changed, and the checker still printed findings.
- c9: The Python duplicate checker, the two Python rule files, and the TypeScript rule files offer no skip-this-path option.

husband-note (gate mechanics — READ BEFORE AUTHORING ORACLES): (1) HERMETIC GATE ENV: aspergillus grades each behavior/metamorphic oracle in a child env whose PATH is only uv/git/bash + system dirs and whose HOME is a fresh scratch dir — cargo/rustc/bun are NOT on PATH by name. Any oracle script that runs cargo (all of these do) MUST prepend: export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH" (mirror the existing scripts/oracles/lib_rust_gate.sh which already does this). Build offline: cargo ... --offline. (2) The C7 metamorphic oracle has relation_class=conservation: it reads the JSON on the runner's STDOUT and requires a `flows` key = a list of signed numbers that must sum to 0 (spec_oracle _relation_conservation) — the EXIT CODE IS NOT THE VERDICT. Encode the exclude conservation as flows=[ +N_without_exclude, -N_with_exclude, -N_lines_under_excluded_path ], which sums to 0 iff excluding the folder removes exactly the findings whose path is under it and nothing else. Emit that JSON from scripts/rust_exclude_conservation_relation.py. (Prior sibling asp-ce6.4 failed its metamorphic ONLY because it emitted no such key and assumed exit-code was the verdict.) (3) The three binaries are aspergillus-rust-dup-type-check, aspergillus-rust-dup-check, aspergillus-rust-gate — all already on the integration branch under rust/; add a repeatable --exclude <glob> (workspace-relative, fnmatch/gitignore-style) to each. rust/src/workspace.rs already skips target/ and hidden dirs — extend that walker with the exclude globs.

This is net-new feature work (a new rule), landed feature-shaped: the fixture tests ARE the outer-loop acceptance per aspergillus's own testing.md ("a rule's e2e is the rule firing on real fixture code").

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. ASP410 lifts the same invariant into the corpus. Same AST-not-text property (exo-8e0): detection is over real cst.Call nodes, so a docstring/comment/string that merely NAMES Dispatcher().tick() is invisible.

CONFIG MECHANISM (the one real design decision). The rule is configurable via three OVERRIDABLE CLASS ATTRIBUTES tuned by subclassing — CONSTRUCT_CLASS_NAMES, DRIVE_METHOD_NAMES, E2E_PATH_PATTERN. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). I did NOT model it on the [tool.aspergillus] extra_io_functions TOML option that the task flagged: verified against source that pebble asp-b72's finding holds — no rule reads that option, it is inert. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

SHAPE. A standard single-file fixit LintRule (no cross-file analysis) as the design discussion concluded. Module-level aggregation: visit_Call accumulates construct nodes and a drive flag, leave_Module reports iff BOTH are present AND the path matches. Detection-only, no autofix (the fix — which real boundary call replaces the in-process construction — is human/agent judgment, same as ASP409); lands at warn per the severity-graduation ADR.

REGISTRATION. Registered in BOTH catalog/__init__.py AND the parent rules/__init__.py re-export. The parent re-export is the load-bearing seam fixit's `enable=["aspergillus.rules"]` walk actually discovers (it does not recurse into the catalog subpackage). A discovery test (test_rule_is_discoverable_by_fixit) asserts collect_rules reaches ASP410.

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/.
