This is net-new feature work (a new rule), landed feature-shaped: the fixture tests ARE the outer-loop acceptance per aspergillus's own testing.md ("a rule's e2e is the rule firing on real fixture code").

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. ASP410 lifts the same invariant into the corpus. Same AST-not-text property (exo-8e0): detection is over real cst.Call nodes, so a docstring/comment/string that merely NAMES Dispatcher().tick() is invisible.

CONFIG MECHANISM (the one real design decision). The rule is configurable via three OVERRIDABLE CLASS ATTRIBUTES tuned by subclassing — CONSTRUCT_CLASS_NAMES, DRIVE_METHOD_NAMES, E2E_PATH_PATTERN. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). I did NOT model it on the [tool.aspergillus] extra_io_functions TOML option that the task flagged: verified against source that pebble asp-b72's finding holds — no rule reads that option, it is inert. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

Module-level aggregation: visit_Call accumulates construct nodes and a drive flag, leave_Module reports iff BOTH are present AND the path matches. Detection-only, no autofix (the fix — which real boundary call replaces the in-process construction — is human/agent judgment, same as ASP409); lands at warn per the severity-graduation ADR.

This is net-new feature work (a new rule), landed feature-shaped: the fixture tests ARE the outer-loop acceptance per aspergillus's own testing.md ("a rule's e2e is the rule firing on real fixture code").

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. ASP410 lifts the same invariant into the corpus. Same AST-not-text property (exo-8e0): detection is over real cst.Call nodes, so a docstring/comment/string that merely NAMES Dispatcher().tick() is invisible.

CONFIG MECHANISM (the one real design decision). The rule is configurable via three OVERRIDABLE CLASS ATTRIBUTES tuned by subclassing — CONSTRUCT_CLASS_NAMES, DRIVE_METHOD_NAMES, E2E_PATH_PATTERN. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). I did NOT model it on the [tool.aspergillus] extra_io_functions TOML option that the task flagged: verified against source that pebble asp-b72's finding holds — no rule reads that option, it is inert. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

SHAPE. A standard single-file fixit LintRule (no cross-file analysis) as the design discussion concluded. Module-level aggregation: visit_Call accumulates construct nodes and a drive flag, leave_Module reports iff BOTH are present AND the path matches. Detection-only, no autofix (the fix — which real boundary call replaces the in-process construction — is human/agent judgment, same as ASP409); lands at warn per the severity-graduation ADR.

REGISTRATION. Registered in BOTH catalog/__init__.py AND the parent rules/__init__.py re-export. The parent re-export is the load-bearing seam fixit's `enable=["aspergillus.rules"]` walk actually discovers (it does not recurse into the catalog subpackage). A discovery test (test_rule_is_discoverable_by_fixit) asserts collect_rules reaches ASP410.

Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria), and the workers refactoring code to satisfy the rules.
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. ASP205 and ASP206 know the imperative shell: a consumer declares which paths are functional core (for example in a config file the gate reads, as TypeScript layouts do), and a function that performs I/O in the shell is legal; I/O inside the declared core is the finding. Their I/O detection no longer matches bare method names that collide with domain methods: `book.open()` on an in-memory book, `json5::read(text)` over a &str, `mpsc` `send`/`recv`, a domain `create`/`accept` constructor are not I/O. ASP204 flags a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`, and does not flag a `loop` whose exit is bounded by a counter or an iterator. Python references: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py (_is_imperative_shell, LowAssertionDensity, ImpureFunction, MixedIOAndLogic), design.md ASP205/206 and TypeScript eslint-plugin-boundaries.

Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).
How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.

payload.description:
Request:
  In the Rust implementation of Aspergillus (the rust/ tree), make rule ASP205 (impure function in the functional core) and rule ASP206 (mixed I/O and logic) correct and blocking.

Both rules must know the imperative shell. A consumer declares which repository paths are the functional core, for example in a config file the gate reads, as the TypeScript layouts do. A function that performs I/O in the imperative shell is legal. I/O inside a declared core path is the finding.

The I/O detection must no longer match bare method names that collide with domain methods. `book.open()` on an in-memory book is not I/O. `json5::read(text)` over a &str is not I/O. An `mpsc` `send` or `recv` is not I/O. A domain `create` or `accept` constructor is not I/O. The detection must find I/O inside closures, for example `iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(..))`. It must find `writeln!` and `write!` to a file. It must find `dbg!`, `flush`, `sync_all` and `std::process::exit`.

Each of the two rules gets committed violating and satisfying fixture pairs that cover the cases above. Each of the two rules is blocking.

Acceptance a person can check without reading code: run the gate over lobaria integrated with `--exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**'` and lobaria's core declaration. These verified false positives produce no finding: shell/src/machine.rs:990 `create`, shell/src/capture.rs:506 `decode_worker` (mpsc send/recv), backtest/src/replay.rs:223 `open_tokens`, chart/src/lib.rs:52 `load` (json5::read), and the ASP206 satisfying fixture's shell wrapper under ASP205. These probes produce an ASP205 finding when a core path declares them: `fn persist(ps: &[&str]) { ps.iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(p, b"").unwrap()); }` and `fn f(w: &mut std::fs::File) { writeln!(w, "x").unwrap(); }`. statechart, which is lobaria's pure core, still has 0 ASP205 findings and 0 ASP206 findings. In rust/, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass. docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe ASP205 and ASP206 as implemented.

Constraints: do not change lobaria's code, because a lobaria pebble applies the rules. Do not change the Python implementation or the TypeScript implementation. Do not port ASP501, ASP502, or other rules that are not yet ported, because a sibling pebble ports those. No report-only mode: each rule is blocking once it is correct.

References: the Python implementation in python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py (`_is_imperative_shell`, `ImpureFunction`, `MixedIOAndLogic`), design.md ASP205 and ASP206, and the TypeScript eslint-plugin-boundaries. It measured ASP206 at 114 findings, about 84% of them in bins, oracles and tests, and at most 11 real core/shell debt items. Priority P1.

payload.description:
Request:

The gate binary reads Rust source files. For each violation the gate prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The gate exits 1 when a rule fires. The gate exits 0 when no rule fires. The gate blocks. No rule is report-only.

An enforced rule runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny.

The gate owns this closed set of single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. Sibling parts add every rule other than ASP303.

Establish the committed fixture layout. Each rule id owns one committed violating fixture and one committed satisfying fixture. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for that rule and exits 0. Commit the fixture pair for ASP303.

Enforce ASP303 in Rust to demonstrate the contract end to end. ASP303 finds an error swallowed into a success value. The Rust forms are `.ok()` that discards an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, and `unwrap_or_default` on a Result.

The Rust column of docs/design.md names the enforcing check for ASP303. That entry does not read 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.

cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.

Prior art: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py.

Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python or TypeScript change. Priority P1.

- c5: The repository holds a sample Rust file that keeps the ASP501 rule.

original_statement:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer can make ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 and ASP206 blocking and every finding is a real instance of the rule's intent, so the rules can gate commits without flagging correct code and without being evaded by common Rust forms.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria), and the workers refactoring code to satisfy the rules.
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. ASP205 and ASP206 know the imperative shell: a consumer declares which paths are functional core (for example in a config file the gate reads, as TypeScript layouts do), and a function that performs I/O in the shell is legal; I/O inside the declared core is the finding. Their I/O detection no longer matches bare method names that collide with domain methods: `book.open()` on an in-memory book, `json5::read(text)` over a &str, `mpsc` `send`/`recv`, a domain `create`/`accept` constructor are not I/O. It sees I/O inside closures (`iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(..))`), `writeln!`/`write!` to a file, `dbg!`, `flush`, `sync_all`, `std::process::exit`. ASP202 follows the Python rule's refinement (asp-070, asp-da5): it scopes to imperative-shell functions, and counts `?`, `return Err(..)` guard clauses, `ok_or`/`ok_or_else`, validating constructors and assert macros as assertions; test functions are exempt as in Python. ASP204 flags a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`, and does not flag a `loop` whose exit is bounded by a counter or an iterator. Every one of the four is blocking and has committed violating and satisfying fixture pairs covering the cases above.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Run over lobaria integrated with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**' and lobaria's core declaration: these verified false positives produce no finding: shell/src/machine.rs:990 `create`, shell/src/capture.rs:506 `decode_worker` (mpsc send/recv), backtest/src/replay.rs:223 `open_tokens`, chart/src/lib.rs:52 `load` (json5::read), statechart/src/array.rs:20 `serialize` (ASP202), and the ASP206 satisfying fixture's shell wrapper under ASP205. These probes produce a finding: `fn persist(ps: &[&str]) { ps.iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(p, b"").unwrap()); }` declared in a core path (ASP205), `fn f(w: &mut std::fs::File) { writeln!(w, "x").unwrap(); }` in core (ASP205), `fn spin() { while true {} }` (ASP204). `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }` produces no ASP204 finding. statechart (lobaria's pure core) still has 0 ASP205 and 0 ASP206 findings. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/; docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe each rule as implemented.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP501/ASP502 or rules not yet ported (a sibling pebble ports those). Not lobaria's code changes (a lobaria pebble applies the rules). Not a Python or TypeScript change. No report-only rule: each of the four is blocking once correct.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP202 1493 findings on lobaria, 1250 (84%) on pure functions, counts only assert!/assert_eq!/assert_ne!/debug_assert*; ASP205 278 findings, 0 in the pure core, >=25 pure functions flagged by name collision, and the crate's own ASP206/satisfying fixture still fires ASP205; ASP206 114 findings, ~84% in bins/oracles/tests, <=11 real FC/IS debt; ASP204 16 findings, 12 bounded by construction, `while true` missed. Python references: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py (_is_imperative_shell, LowAssertionDensity, ImpureFunction, MixedIOAndLogic), design.md ASP205/206 and TypeScript eslint-plugin-boundaries.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: In the Rust implementation of Aspergillus (the rust/ tree), make rule ASP202 (low assertion density) correct and blocking. Follow the refinement the Python rule received in asp-070 and asp-da5.
  ASP202 scopes to imperative-shell functions. It reads the consumer's declaration of which repository paths are the functional core, the same declaration ASP205 and ASP206 read. ASP202 counts these forms as assertions: the `?` operator, a `return Err(..)` guard clause, `ok_or`, `ok_or_else`, a validating constructor, and the assert macros. Test functions are exempt, as they are in Python.
  ASP202 gets committed violating and satisfying fixture pairs that cover the cases above. ASP202 is blocking.
  Acceptance a person can check without reading code: run the gate over lobaria integrated with `--exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**'` and lobaria's core declaration. The verified false positive statechart/src/array.rs:20 `serialize` produces no ASP202 finding. In rust/, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass. docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe ASP202 as implemented.
  Constraints: do not change lobaria's code, because a lobaria pebble applies the rules. Do not change the Python implementation or the TypeScript implementation. Do not port ASP501, ASP502, or other rules that are not yet ported, because a sibling pebble ports those. No report-only mode: ASP202 is blocking once it is correct.
  References: the Python implementation in python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py (`_is_imperative_shell`, `LowAssertionDensity`) and design.md. The 2026-09-23 verification (cloud agents VerifyASP202 and VerifyLobariaGate, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) measured ASP202 at 1493 findings on lobaria, 1250 of them (84%) on pure functions, and counted only assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne! and debug_assert*. Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Make the Rust ASP202 low-assertion-density rule scope to imperative-shell code, count the Rust assertion forms, exempt tests, ship fixture pairs, and run as a blocking check.

restatement:
  Aspergillus checks the ASP rules on Rust source in the rust/ tree. The ASP202 rule measures assertion density. Today the Rust ASP202 rule is too blunt. A measurement on 2026-09-23 ran it over lobaria and got 1493 findings. 1250 of those findings (84 percent) sat on pure functions. The rule counted only assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne! and the debug_assert macros. A person verified one of the false findings at statechart/src/array.rs line 20, on the function serialize.
  This request gives the Rust ASP202 rule the same refinement the Python rule got in asp-070 and asp-da5.
  First, scope. ASP202 applies only to a function in the imperative shell. The consumer declares which repository paths hold its functional core. ASP202 reads that declaration. ASP205 and ASP206 read the same declaration. A function inside a declared core path gets no ASP202 finding.
  Second, counting. ASP202 counts each of these Rust forms as an assertion: the ? operator, a return Err(..) guard clause, ok_or, ok_or_else, a validating constructor, and the assert macros.
  Third, tests. A test function gets no ASP202 finding. The Python rule exempts test functions in the same way.
  Fourth, evidence. The repository carries committed Rust fixture pairs. Each pair has one file that breaks the rule and one file that obeys it. The pairs cover the core scope case, each assertion form above, and the test exemption.
  Fifth, severity. ASP202 is blocking. A run that finds an ASP202 violation fails. ASP202 has no report-only mode.
  A person checks the result without reading code. The person runs the Rust gate over the integrated lobaria workspace. The person passes --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' and --exclude 'vendored/**', and lobaria's own core declaration. The gate reports no ASP202 finding on statechart/src/array.rs line 20, the function serialize. In the rust/ tree, cargo test passes, cargo clippy with -D warnings passes, and cargo fmt --check passes. docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe ASP202 as implemented and blocking. Neither document still calls it manual, planned, or report-only.
  The work stays inside the Rust tree, its fixtures, and the documents. It changes no file of lobaria, because a separate lobaria pebble applies the rules there. It changes no file of the Python implementation and no file of the TypeScript implementation. It ports no further rule: ASP501, ASP502 and the other unported rules belong to a sibling pebble.

restatement:
  Today the rust/ directory of Aspergillus holds a README and two config files. No Aspergillus program reads a Rust source file. A Rust consumer therefore gets no Aspergillus finding. This request builds the first mechanical Rust surface, and proves the contract with one rule.
  The deliverable is a gate program that lives in the rust/ tree. The gate reads Rust source files. For each violation the gate prints one line. The line has the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The gate exits with status 1 when a rule fires. The gate exits with status 0 when no rule fires. The gate blocks a commit. No rule is report-only. An enforced rule runs from the gate program itself, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny.
  The gate owns a closed set of 18 single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. This part implements one of them, ASP303. Sibling parts add the other 17. The closed set is written down here, because the sibling parts read it.
  This part also establishes the committed fixture layout that every sibling part follows. Each rule id owns one committed fixture that breaks the rule, and one committed fixture that obeys it. Running the gate over the breaking fixture prints that rule id, and the run fails. Running the gate over the obeying fixture prints nothing for that rule, and the run passes. This part commits the fixture pair for ASP303, and records the layout so a sibling part can copy it.
  ASP303 finds an error swallowed into a success value. The Rust forms are three: `.ok()` that discards an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, and `unwrap_or_default` on a Result. The Python rule ErrorSwallowedIntoSentinel in python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py is the prior art for the intent.
  The Rust column of the ASP303 row in docs/design.md names the enforcing check. That cell today reads a dash. After this change the cell does not read 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays clean in rust/: cargo test passes, cargo clippy with -D warnings reports no problem, and cargo fmt --check reports no problem.
  This part does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling part fixes those. This part changes no Python rule and no TypeScript rule.

  Aspergillus today ships Rust support as configuration files only. The rust/ directory holds a clippy.toml and a cargo-lints.toml. It holds no gate program. Maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus therefore get no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog and verification-integrity rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable: a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`, that blocks on the ASP4xx rules. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints exactly one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation it finds. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule may be implemented inside the gate program, or it may be implemented as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny and whose output the gate reports in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Either way the rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named rules have a direct Rust analogue, so the gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be fused into one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer or an environment branch that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that claims to be an end-to-end test.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves it deliberately unassigned, and catalog/__init__.py records why. Rust still needs an entry for it. That entry is either an enforcing check or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary, for example a property the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture lives at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture lives at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Run over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Run over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Its Rust column names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason, for each of ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409 and ASP410. No entry for any of those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. It does not change the Python surface. It does not change the TypeScript surface.

How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. Running the Rust duplicate-type check over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` in one crate and `struct Balance(pub u64)` in another reports BOTH as a structural duplicate (same skeleton, different name). Over a probe with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` in one crate and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` in another reports BOTH (field reorder is still a duplicate). Each finding prints path:line: ASP502 and the check exits 1; a genuinely distinct type shape produces nothing. ASP502 remains blocking (exit 1 on a finding). Its shape fingerprint becomes order-insensitive over field/variant NAMES and TYPES so a rename or reorder no longer evades it, while distinct shapes still do not collide.

goal: Make the Rust ASP502 duplicate-type check report a struct or enum that another crate duplicates under a different name, or with its fields or variants in a different order, with committed fixtures and a green Rust toolchain.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust duplicate-type check that reports the rule ASP502 over a Cargo workspace. Today the check groups two declarations only when they carry the SAME declared name, and its shape fingerprint keeps the ORDERED list of field names or variant names. A person therefore evades the check with a rename, or with a reorder of the fields. A cloud agent named VerifyDupRules confirmed both evasions on 2026-09-23. This request removes both evasions. The check must report a struct or an enum that a second crate declares under a DIFFERENT name with the same shape. The check must also report a struct or an enum whose fields or variants stand in a different order. The shape fingerprint becomes order-insensitive over the field and variant NAMES and TYPES, and the check stops keying a group on the declared name. The concrete demonstration is a two-crate probe: one crate declares `struct Lamports(pub u64)`, the other declares `struct Balance(pub u64)`, and the check names BOTH. A second two-crate probe declares `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` in one crate and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` in the other, and the check names BOTH. The wider fingerprint must not collide two genuinely distinct type shapes: a distinct shape still produces no finding. The check keeps everything it does today. It still finds the same-name same-ordered-shape duplicate across crates. It still honours `--allowlist FILE`. It still requires the duplicate to cross a crate boundary, so two identical types inside ONE crate stay unreported. Every finding keeps the existing text `path:line: ASP502`. The check stays blocking: it exits 1 when it reports a finding. The repository carries a committed violating fixture pair and a committed satisfying fixture pair, and the violating pair covers the renamed case and the reordered case. The Rust toolchain stays clean: cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check all pass in rust/. The request changes no Python code and no TypeScript code, and it does not touch ASP501, which the sibling pebble asp-2d6.2 owns. The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus, and the first consumer is lobaria. This work corrects an under-coverage of asp-2d6, whose decomposition omitted the ASP502 enhancement that the root filing names.

original_statement:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer gets the whole Aspergillus rule set, not a subset: every ASP rule id that exists for Python has a blocking Rust check with fixtures, or docs/design.md states why the rule does not apply to Rust.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. docs/design.md Rust column: no entry reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id listed above. For every enforced rule, running the gate over its violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1, and over its satisfying fixture prints nothing for it and exits 0. ASP502 over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` and `struct Balance(pub u64)` reports both; with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` reports both. ASP501 over a probe with a 6-statement block copied into two otherwise different functions reports both. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP202/204/205/206 (a sibling pebble fixes those). No report-only rule: every enforced rule blocks. Not a Python or TypeScript change. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable if it is exophial-specific.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304), rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417), python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py and __main__.py check-duplicates (fragment + type-1 passes). Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP501 is whole-body only and misses copied statement spines; ASP502 misses a renamed duplicate and a field reorder; ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: Give the Rust ASP203 check a committed violating fixture and a committed satisfying fixture. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  Acceptance: ASP203 has a fixture pair. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints `path:line: ASP203` and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for ASP203 and exits 0. The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The check blocks.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. No report-only behavior; the check blocks. This is not a Python or TypeScript change.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Commit a violating fixture crate and a satisfying fixture crate for the Rust ASP203 rule, and show that the Aspergillus Rust gate prints `path:line: ASP203` and fails over the first crate, and prints no ASP203 line and passes over the second crate.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Every other Rust rule that has a check also has two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/lib.rs`. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check itself runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

restatement_clauses:
- C1: A violating fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/Cargo.toml`.
- C2: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/src/lib.rs` declares global mutable state with `static mut`.
- C3: A satisfying fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/Cargo.toml`.
- C4: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` exists, so the gate has real Rust code to read in the satisfying crate.
- C5: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` declares no `static mut`.
- C6: Git tracks the files of both fixture crates: at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`, so both crates are committed and not untracked working files.
- C7: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203` and exits with status 1, so the ASP203 finding blocks and is not report-only.
- C8: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` prints no line for ASP203 and exits with status 0.
- C9: `cargo test` passes in `rust/` for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`, and its tests catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code.
- C10: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` both pass in `rust/`.

acceptance_criteria:
- C1: The sample Rust crate that breaks the global-mutable-state rule carries its own package file, so a person can point the checker at a real crate.
- C2: The source file of the sample crate that breaks the rule keeps a global mutable value.
- C3: The second sample Rust crate, the one that follows the global-mutable-state rule, carries its own package file.
- C4: The sample Rust crate that follows the rule carries a source file, so the checker has real code to read.
- C5: The source file of the sample crate that follows the rule keeps no global mutable value.
- C6: A person asks the repository which files it keeps for each of the two sample crates. The repository lists at least two files for the crate that breaks the rule. It lists at least two files for the crate that follows the rule.
- C7: A person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample crate that breaks the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints at least one line that names the file, then the line number, then ASP203. The run fails with status 1.
- C8: The same person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample crate that follows the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints no ASP203 line. The run passes with status 0.
- C9: The Rust test suite of the checker passes. It is strong enough that a deliberate break in the changed checker code makes a test fail.
- C10: A person runs the Rust formatting check and the Rust lint check over the repository's Rust code. The formatting check reports no change to make. The lint check reports no warning.

No rule is report-only.

Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/lib.rs`. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.

The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.

  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. - C3: The repository holds the package file of the second sample Rust project, the one that follows the global-mutable-state rule.
- C4: The sample Rust project that follows the rule carries a source file, so the checker has real code to read.
- C5: The source file of the sample project that follows the rule keeps no global value that any code can change.
- C6: A person asks the repository which files it keeps for each of the two sample projects. The repository lists at least two files for the project that breaks the rule. It lists at least two files for the project that follows the rule.

A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check itself runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Every other Rust rule that has a check also has two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/lib.rs`. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.

The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check itself runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.

Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds configs and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

original_statement:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer gets the whole Aspergillus rule set, not a subset: every ASP rule id that exists for Python has a blocking Rust check with fixtures, or docs/design.md states why the rule does not apply to Rust.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. docs/design.md Rust column: no entry reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id listed above. For every enforced rule, running the gate over its violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1, and over its satisfying fixture prints nothing for it and exits 0. ASP502 over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` and `struct Balance(pub u64)` reports both; with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` reports both. ASP501 over a probe with a 6-statement block copied into two otherwise different functions reports both. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP202/204/205/206 (a sibling pebble fixes those). No report-only rule: every enforced rule blocks. Not a Python or TypeScript change. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable if it is exophial-specific.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304), rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417), python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py and __main__.py check-duplicates (fragment + type-1 passes). Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP501 is whole-body only and misses copied statement spines; ASP502 misses a renamed duplicate and a field reorder; ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: Give the Rust ASP203 check a committed violating fixture and a committed satisfying fixture. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  Acceptance: ASP203 has a fixture pair. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints `path:line: ASP203` and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for ASP203 and exits 0. The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The check blocks.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. No report-only behavior; the check blocks. This is not a Python or TypeScript change.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Commit a violating fixture crate and a satisfying fixture crate for the Rust ASP203 rule, and show that the Aspergillus Rust gate prints `path:line: ASP203` and fails over the first crate, and prints no ASP203 line and passes over the second crate.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Every other Rust rule that has a check also has two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` and a `src/lib.rs`. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate expresses the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check itself runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: A violating fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/Cargo.toml`.
- c2: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/src/lib.rs` declares global mutable state with `static mut`.
- c3: A satisfying fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/Cargo.toml`.
- c4: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` exists, so the gate has real Rust code to read in the satisfying crate.
- c5: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` declares no `static mut`.
- c6: Git tracks the files of both fixture crates: at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`, so both crates are committed and not untracked working files.
- c7: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203` and exits with status 1, so the ASP203 finding blocks and is not report-only.
- c8: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` prints no line for ASP203 and exits with status 0.
- c9: `cargo test` passes in `rust/` for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`, and its tests catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code.
- c10: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` both pass in `rust/`.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: The repository holds the package file of the sample Rust project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule, at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/Cargo.toml`.
- c2: The source file of the sample project that breaks the rule keeps a global value that any code can change: `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/src/lib.rs` declares `static mut`.
- c3: The repository holds the package file of the second sample Rust project, the one that follows the global-mutable-state rule, at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/Cargo.toml`.
- c4: The sample Rust project that follows the rule carries a source file at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs`, so the checker has real code to read.
- c5: The source file of the sample project that follows the rule keeps no global value that any code can change: `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` declares no `static mut`.
- c6: A person asks the repository which files it keeps for each of the two sample projects. The repository lists at least two files for the project that breaks the rule. It lists at least two files for the project that follows the rule.
- c7: A person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints at least one line that names the file, then the line number, then ASP203. Every ASP203 line it prints carries that form. The run fails with status 1.
- c8: The same person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that follows the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints no ASP203 line. The run passes with status 0.
- c9: The Rust test suite of the checker passes. It is strong enough that a deliberate break in the changed checker code makes a test fail.
- c10: A person runs the Rust formatting check and the Rust lint check over the repository's Rust code. The formatting check reports no change to make. The lint check reports no warning.

original_statement:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer gets the whole Aspergillus rule set, not a subset: every ASP rule id that exists for Python has a blocking Rust check with fixtures, or docs/design.md states why the rule does not apply to Rust.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).

A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.

Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell.   This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds configs and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

- c4: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that walks one list several times to add up several totals, then over the stored good example that walks the list one time. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP406 for each file, and whether it refused each run.

- c6: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that hides a hardcoded answer, or a branch on the environment, then over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP408 for each file, and whether it refused each run.
- c7: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that starts its own package in a separate process, then over the stored good example that calls the package directly. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP409 for each file, and whether it refused each run.

- c12: Run the Rust linter with warnings treated as errors, and run the Rust formatter in check mode, both in the rust/ directory. A report states the result of each one.

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). goal: Commit a violating fixture crate and a satisfying fixture crate for the Rust ASP203 rule, and show that the Aspergillus Rust gate prints `path:line: ASP203` and fails over the first crate, and prints no ASP203 line and passes over the second crate.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Every other Rust rule that has a check also has two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` file and a `src/lib.rs` file. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires on a real violation. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate does the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate prints no ASP203 line in any other form. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

- c3: A satisfying fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/Cargo.toml`.
- c4: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` exists, so the gate has real Rust code to read in the satisfying crate.
- c5: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` declares no `static mut`.
- c6: Git tracks the files of both fixture crates: at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`, so both crates are committed and not untracked working files.
- c7: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`, prints no ASP203 line in any other form, and exits with status 1, so the ASP203 finding blocks and is not report-only.
- c8: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` prints no line for ASP203 and exits with status 0.
- c9: `cargo test` passes in `rust/` for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`, and its tests catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code.
- c10: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` both pass in `rust/`.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: The repository holds the package file of the sample Rust project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule.
- c2: The source file of the sample project that breaks the rule keeps a global value that any code can change.
- c3: The repository holds the package file of the second sample Rust project, the one that follows the global-mutable-state rule.
- c4: The sample Rust project that follows the rule carries a source file, so the checker has real code to read.
- c5: The source file of the sample project that follows the rule keeps no global value that any code can change.
- c6: A person asks the repository which files it keeps for each of the two sample projects. The repository lists at least two files for the project that breaks the rule. It lists at least two files for the project that follows the rule.
- c7: A person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints at least one line that names the file, then the line number, then ASP203. Every ASP203 line it prints carries that form. The run fails with status 1.
- c8: The same person runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that follows the global-mutable-state rule. The checker prints no ASP203 line. The run passes with status 0.
- c9: The Rust test suite of the checker passes. It is strong enough that a deliberate break in the changed checker code makes a test fail.
- c10: A person runs the Rust formatting check and the Rust lint check over the repository's Rust code. The formatting check reports no change to make. The lint check reports no warning.
