  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer gets the whole Aspergillus rule set, not a subset: every ASP rule id that exists for Python has a blocking Rust check with fixtures, or docs/design.md states why the rule does not apply to Rust.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. docs/design.md Rust column: no entry reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id listed above. For every enforced rule, running the gate over its violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1, and over its satisfying fixture prints nothing for it and exits 0. ASP502 over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` and `struct Balance(pub u64)` reports both; with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` reports both. ASP501 over a probe with a 6-statement block copied into two otherwise different functions reports both. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP202/204/205/206 (a sibling pebble fixes those). No report-only rule: every enforced rule blocks. Not a Python or TypeScript change. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable if it is exophial-specific.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304), rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417), python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py and __main__.py check-duplicates (fragment + type-1 passes). Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP501 is whole-body only and misses copied statement spines; ASP502 misses a renamed duplicate and a field reorder; ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: Give a Rust consumer a blocking check for every single-file Aspergillus rule that exists for Python. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  The Rust column of docs/design.md must name an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. In place of a check, the column may give a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. The reason must name the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary, for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable, because it is exophial-specific.
  No entry in the Rust column reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id in that list.
  Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. Each enforced rule prints `path:line: ASPnnn`. Each enforced rule blocks. Each enforced rule has a committed violating fixture and a committed satisfying fixture. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for that rule and exits 0.
  Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced. Examples: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. No rule is report-only; every enforced rule blocks. This is not a Python or TypeScript change.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Prior art: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304) and rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417).
  Priority P1.
  Decomposed child: Build a blocking gate for Rust source files in the rust/ directory of the Aspergillus repository. Today rust/ holds configs and a README only. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  The gate binary reads Rust source files. For each violation the gate prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The gate exits 1 when a rule fires. The gate exits 0 when no rule fires. The gate blocks. No rule is report-only.
  An enforced rule runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny.
  The gate owns this closed set of single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. Sibling parts add every rule other than ASP303.
  Establish the committed fixture layout. Each rule id owns one committed violating fixture and one committed satisfying fixture. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for that rule and exits 0. Commit the fixture pair for ASP303.
  Enforce ASP303 in Rust to demonstrate the contract end to end. ASP303 finds an error swallowed into a success value. The Rust forms are `.ok()` that discards an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, and `unwrap_or_default` on a Result.
  The Rust column of docs/design.md names the enforcing check for ASP303. That entry does not read 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Prior art: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python or TypeScript change. Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Add a blocking Rust source gate under rust/ named aspergillus-gate. The gate prints `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation and exits 1 when a rule fires. The gate declares the closed set of 18 single-file rule ids, establishes the committed violating/satisfying fixture layout, and enforces ASP303 end to end.

restatement:
  The Aspergillus repository must gain a blocking gate for Rust source files. The gate lives in the rust/ directory. That directory today holds a configs directory and a README only. The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  The gate is a Rust program. The cargo crate root is rust/. The cargo package and the binary carry the same name, `aspergillus-gate`. The gate's own Rust sources live under rust/src. The gate reads Rust source files. For each violation the gate prints one line. That line has the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The gate exits 1 when a rule fires. The gate exits 0 when no rule fires. The gate blocks in every case. No rule is report-only. A rule counts as enforced when it runs from the gate binary, or when it runs from a clippy lint that the gate forces at the deny level.
  The gate owns a closed set of 18 single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. This part declares the whole set in the gate's sources under rust/src. This part implements ASP303 only. Sibling parts add every rule other than ASP303.
  This part also establishes the committed fixture layout. Each rule id owns one committed violating fixture and one committed satisfying fixture. This part commits the fixture pair for ASP303. The violating fixture is `rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs`. The satisfying fixture is `rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs`. The gate over the violating fixture prints ASP303 and exits 1. The gate over the satisfying fixture prints no ASP303 line and exits 0.
  ASP303 finds an error that the code swallows into a success value. The Rust forms are three. The first form is `.ok()` that discards an Err. The second form is `let _ =` on a Result. The third form is `unwrap_or_default` on a Result. The gate flags all three forms. The violating fixture carries all three forms.
  The Rust column of docs/design.md names `aspergillus-gate` as the enforcing check for ASP303. Today that column reads `—`. That table row must not read 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain gates pass in rust/. `cargo test` passes. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes. The `cargo test` suite must be adequate. It must fail when the gate's own logic changes.
  The Python rules file python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py is the prior art for ASP303. This part changes no Python code and no TypeScript code. This part does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling part fixes those.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: Every violation line the gate prints has the form `path:line: ASPnnn`.
- c2: The gate's Rust sources under rust/src declare the closed set of 18 single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417.
- c3: The repository commits a violating fixture for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs.
- c4: The repository commits a satisfying fixture for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs.
- c5: The gate over rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs prints at least one ASP303 line and exits 1.
- c6: The gate over rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs prints no ASP303 line and exits 0.
- c7: ASP303 flags all three Rust forms of a swallowed error: `.ok()` that discards an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, and `unwrap_or_default` on a Result.
- c8: The Rust column of the ASP303 table row in docs/design.md names `aspergillus-gate` as the enforcing check.
- c9: The ASP303 table row in docs/design.md does not read 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
- c10: `cargo test` passes for the `aspergillus-gate` package in rust/, and the suite fails when the gate's own logic changes.
- c11: `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass in rust/.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: A person runs the new Rust checker over the stored bad example for ASP303. The checker reports at least one problem. Every reported line reads as a file path, then a colon, then a line number, then a colon, then a space, then a rule name such as ASP303. No reported line reads any other way.
- c2: The Rust sources of the new checker, under rust/src, carry the names of the eighteen checks the checker owns. All eighteen names appear there.
- c3: The repository holds the bad example file for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs.
- c4: The repository holds the good example file for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs.
- c5: A person runs the new Rust checker over the stored bad example for ASP303. At least one reported line names ASP303. The checker finishes with a failure status of 1.
- c6: A person runs the new Rust checker over the stored good example for ASP303. No reported line names ASP303. The checker finishes with a success status of 0.
- c7: A person writes three small Rust files. Each file holds exactly one of the three named mistakes: dropping an error with .ok(), throwing an error away with let _ =, and replacing an error with a default value through unwrap_or_default. The person runs the new Rust checker over each file. The checker names ASP303 for all three files.
- c8: The table row for ASP303 in docs/design.md names aspergillus-gate in its last column, the Rust one, as the thing that enforces the rule.
- c9: The table row for ASP303 in docs/design.md does not say 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
- c10: The automatic tests of the new Rust package all pass. The tests also catch small deliberate changes made to the new code, so a test that checks nothing cannot pass this.
- c11: In the rust/ directory a person runs the Rust style checker with warnings treated as errors. The person then runs the Rust formatter in check mode. Both finish with a success status of 0.

original_statement:
  In one sentence, what is the user-facing outcome you want? A Rust consumer can make ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 and ASP206 blocking and every finding is a real instance of the rule's intent, so the rules can gate commits without flagging correct code and without being evaded by common Rust forms.
  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria), and the workers refactoring code to satisfy the rules.
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. ASP205 and ASP206 know the imperative shell: a consumer declares which paths are functional core (for example in a config file the gate reads, as TypeScript layouts do), and a function that performs I/O in the shell is legal; I/O inside the declared core is the finding. Their I/O detection no longer matches bare method names that collide with domain methods: `book.open()` on an in-memory book, `json5::read(text)` over a &str, `mpsc` `send`/`recv`, a domain `create`/`accept` constructor are not I/O. It sees I/O inside closures (`iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(..))`), `writeln!`/`write!` to a file, `dbg!`, `flush`, `sync_all`, `std::process::exit`. ASP202 follows the Python rule's refinement (asp-070, asp-da5): it scopes to imperative-shell functions, and counts `?`, `return Err(..)` guard clauses, `ok_or`/`ok_or_else`, validating constructors and assert macros as assertions; test functions are exempt as in Python. ASP204 flags a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`, and does not flag a `loop` whose exit is bounded by a counter or an iterator. Every one of the four is blocking and has committed violating and satisfying fixture pairs covering the cases above.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. Run over lobaria integrated with --exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**' and lobaria's core declaration: these verified false positives produce no finding: shell/src/machine.rs:990 `create`, shell/src/capture.rs:506 `decode_worker` (mpsc send/recv), backtest/src/replay.rs:223 `open_tokens`, chart/src/lib.rs:52 `load` (json5::read), statechart/src/array.rs:20 `serialize` (ASP202), and the ASP206 satisfying fixture's shell wrapper under ASP205. These probes produce a finding: `fn persist(ps: &[&str]) { ps.iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(p, b"").unwrap()); }` declared in a core path (ASP205), `fn f(w: &mut std::fs::File) { writeln!(w, "x").unwrap(); }` in core (ASP205), `fn spin() { while true {} }` (ASP204). `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }` produces no ASP204 finding. statechart (lobaria's pure core) still has 0 ASP205 and 0 ASP206 findings. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/; docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe each rule as implemented.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP501/ASP502 or rules not yet ported (a sibling pebble ports those). Not lobaria's code changes (a lobaria pebble applies the rules). Not a Python or TypeScript change. No report-only rule: each of the four is blocking once correct.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP202 1493 findings on lobaria, 1250 (84%) on pure functions, counts only assert!/assert_eq!/assert_ne!/debug_assert*; ASP205 278 findings, 0 in the pure core, >=25 pure functions flagged by name collision, and the crate's own ASP206/satisfying fixture still fires ASP205; ASP206 114 findings, ~84% in bins/oracles/tests, <=11 real FC/IS debt; ASP204 16 findings, 12 bounded by construction, `while true` missed. Python references: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level2.py (_is_imperative_shell, LowAssertionDensity, ImpureFunction, MixedIOAndLogic), design.md ASP205/206 and TypeScript eslint-plugin-boundaries.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: In the Rust implementation of Aspergillus (the rust/ tree), make rule ASP204 (unbounded loop) correct and blocking.
  ASP204 flags a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`. ASP204 does not flag a `loop` whose exit is bounded by a counter or by an iterator.
  ASP204 gets committed violating and satisfying fixture pairs that cover the cases above. ASP204 is blocking.
  Acceptance a person can check without reading code: run the gate over lobaria integrated with `--exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**'`. The probe `fn spin() { while true {} }` produces an ASP204 finding. The probe `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }` produces no ASP204 finding. In rust/, `cargo test`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass. docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md describe ASP204 as implemented.
  Constraints: do not change lobaria's code, because a lobaria pebble applies the rules. Do not change the Python implementation or the TypeScript implementation. Do not port ASP501, ASP502, or other rules that are not yet ported, because a sibling pebble ports those. No report-only mode: ASP204 is blocking once it is correct.
  References: design.md ASP204. The 2026-09-23 verification (cloud agents VerifySingleFileRules and VerifyLobariaGate, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) measured ASP204 at 16 findings on lobaria, 12 of them bounded by construction, and it found that `while true` was missed. Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Make the Rust gate's ASP204 rule flag only a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`, keep it silent on a `loop` bounded by a counter or by an iterator, commit violating and satisfying fixture pairs for those cases, keep ASP204 blocking, and update docs/design.md and docs/rust-rules.md to match.

restatement:
  The Rust tree of Aspergillus holds a Cargo crate, `aspergillus-rust-gate`. The gate reports each finding as `path:line: ASPnnn`. Rule ASP204 is the "unbounded loop" rule. Today the Rust ASP204 rule is wrong in two directions. It flags every `loop { ... }` construct, so it reports a loop that a counter bounds and a loop that an iterator bounds. It also misses `while true`, which is the exact pattern the rule exists to catch. The 2026-09-23 verification measured this: ASP204 produced 16 findings on lobaria, and 12 of the 16 were on loops that are bounded by construction.
  This request makes ASP204 correct, and keeps it blocking.
  Correct means two things. First, ASP204 reports a finding on a loop whose iteration count a reader cannot determine from the source alone. `while true` is one such loop, and ASP204 must report it. Second, ASP204 reports no finding on a loop whose exit a counter bounds, and no finding on a loop whose exit an iterator bounds. Those loops are bounded by construction.
  The repository stores the evidence for both directions as committed Rust fixtures under `rust/fixtures/ASP204/`. Each covered case gets a pair. One file of the pair breaks the rule. The other file of the pair obeys the rule. The gate reports at least one ASP204 finding on the first file. The gate reports no ASP204 finding on the second file. The pairs cover `while true`, a `loop` that a counter bounds, and a `loop` that an iterator bounds.
  Blocking means one ASP204 finding makes the gate run fail. The gate exits with a non-zero status. There is no report-only setting and no warning-only setting for ASP204.
  A person checks the result on real code. The person runs the gate over lobaria with the two exclude globs `scripts/oracles/fixtures/**` and `vendored/**`. The repository keeps a verbatim committed copy of lobaria under `rust/fixtures/lobaria-<sha>/`, with a PROVENANCE.md, so the same run repeats without a second checkout. Inside that run, a probe file that holds `fn spin() { while true {} }` produces an ASP204 finding. A probe file that holds `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }` produces no ASP204 finding. The gate changes no file it reads.
  The Rust crate stays healthy. In `rust/`, `cargo test` passes, `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes, and `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The two documents describe ASP204 as it now behaves. The ASP204 row in docs/design.md no longer calls the Rust side "Manual", "planned", or a matter of module structure. The file docs/rust-rules.md carries a Markdown heading that names ASP204. Under that heading the text names `while true`, names the counter bound, names the iterator bound, and says the rule is blocking.
  The work stays inside this scope. It does not change lobaria's own source, because a separate lobaria pebble applies the rules there. It does not change the Python implementation or the TypeScript implementation. It does not port ASP501, ASP502, or any other rule that the gate does not carry today, because a sibling pebble owns those.

restatement_clauses:
- C1: ASP204 reports a finding on a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`. In a gate run over lobaria with `--exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**'`, the probe `fn spin() { while true {} }` produces at least one ASP204 finding.
- C2: ASP204 reports no finding on a `loop` whose exit a counter bounds. In the same gate run, the probe `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }` produces no ASP204 finding, while the `while true` probe still produces one.
- C3: The repository holds committed ASP204 violating and satisfying Rust fixture pairs under `rust/fixtures/ASP204/` that cover `while true`, a `loop` bounded by a counter, and a `loop` bounded by an iterator. The gate reports at least one ASP204 finding on every violating fixture and no ASP204 finding on every satisfying fixture.
- C4: ASP204 is blocking and has no report-only mode. One ASP204 finding makes the gate exit with a non-zero status, and the same gate exits zero on the matching satisfying fixture.
- C5: The gate runs to completion over the committed verbatim copy of lobaria under `rust/fixtures/lobaria-<sha>/` with `--exclude 'scripts/oracles/fixtures/**' --exclude 'vendored/**'`, it reads at least five Rust files of that copy, and it changes no file of that copy.
- C6: In `rust/`, `cargo test` passes for the `aspergillus-rust-gate` package, and the tests catch every deliberate change to the code they cover.
- C7: In `rust/`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes with zero warnings, and `cargo fmt --check` passes.
- C8: The ASP204 entry in docs/design.md no longer describes the Rust side as "Manual", "planned", or module structure.
- C9: The docs/rust-rules.md section headed ASP204 describes the rule as implemented: it names `while true`, names the counter bound, names the iterator bound, and says the rule is blocking.
- C10: The Python implementation and the TypeScript implementation keep their behaviour. The Python rule suite and the TypeScript rule suite each report zero failures.
- C11: This work ports no further rule. In the same lobaria gate run, the gate reports no ASP501 finding and no ASP502 finding.

acceptance_criteria:
- C1: A report runs the Rust checker over the stored copy of the lobaria code, skipping the two folders the request names, with a small added Rust file that holds the function `fn spin() { while true {} }`. The report counts the unbounded-loop findings on that added file. The count is at least one.
- C2: The same report also adds a small Rust file that holds the counting loop `loop { if n >= 10 { break; } n += 1; }`. It counts the unbounded-loop findings on that file. The count is zero, while the endless-loop file in the same run still gives at least one finding.
- C3: A report runs the Rust checker over each stored pair of Rust example files that the project keeps for the unbounded-loop rule. It counts the pairs it checked, the bad examples that gave no finding, the good examples that gave a finding, the example files it could not find, and the required situations that no pair covers. At least three pairs were checked, and all four other counts are zero.
- C4: A report runs the Rust checker twice: once over the stored bad example of the unbounded-loop rule, and once over the stored good example. It states the finish status of each run and the number of unbounded-loop findings on the bad example. The run over the bad example failed and gave at least one finding. The run over the good example succeeded.
- C5: A report states whether the checker finished its run over the stored lobaria copy with the two folders skipped, how many Rust files of that copy it read, and how many files of that copy changed while it ran. The checker finished, it read at least five Rust files, and it changed no file.
- C6: The Rust test suite of the checker passes, and those tests notice every deliberate change made to the code they cover.
- C7: A report runs the Rust style check and the Rust formatting check over the Rust tree and states the result of each. The style check finished with zero warnings. The formatting check finished with no complaint.
- C8: No line of the design document that mentions the unbounded-loop rule still calls its Rust handling manual, planned, or a matter of module structure.
- C9: The Rust rule document describes the unbounded-loop rule as built: the text under its heading names the endless `while true` loop, the counter that bounds a loop, the iterator that bounds a loop, and the fact that the rule blocks a run. All four facts are present.
- C10: A report runs the existing Python rule tests and the existing TypeScript rule tests and counts the failures in each. Both counts are zero.
- C11: A report counts the findings the checker reported for rule ASP501 and for rule ASP502 in the run over the stored lobaria copy, and states whether the checker finished. Both counts are zero, and the checker finished.

  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria), and the workers refactoring code to satisfy the rules.
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. ASP205 and ASP206 know the imperative shell: a consumer declares which paths are functional core (for example in a config file the gate reads, as TypeScript layouts do), and a function that performs I/O in the shell is legal; I/O inside the declared core is the finding. Their I/O detection no longer matches bare method names that collide with domain methods: `book.open()` on an in-memory book, `json5::read(text)` over a &str, `mpsc` `send`/`recv`, a domain `create`/`accept` constructor are not I/O. It sees I/O inside closures (`iter().for_each(|p| std::fs::write(..))`), `writeln!`/`write!` to a file, `dbg!`, `flush`, `sync_all`, `std::process::exit`. ASP202 follows the Python rule's refinement (asp-070, asp-da5): it scopes to imperative-shell functions, and counts `?`, `return Err(..)` guard clauses, `ok_or`/`ok_or_else`, validating constructors and assert macros as assertions; test functions are exempt as in Python. ASP204 flags a loop with no statically determinable bound, including `while true`, and does not flag a `loop` whose exit is bounded by a counter or an iterator. restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds configs and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

original_statement:

  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. docs/design.md Rust column: no entry reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id listed above. For every enforced rule, running the gate over its violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1, and over its satisfying fixture prints nothing for it and exits 0. ASP502 over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` and `struct Balance(pub u64)` reports both; with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` reports both. ASP501 over a probe with a 6-statement block copied into two otherwise different functions reports both. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP202/204/205/206 (a sibling pebble fixes those). No report-only rule: every enforced rule blocks. Not a Python or TypeScript change. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable if it is exophial-specific.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304), rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417), python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py and __main__.py check-duplicates (fragment + type-1 passes).   What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: Give a Rust consumer a blocking check for every single-file Aspergillus rule that exists for Python. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  The Rust column of docs/design.md must name an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. In place of a check, the column may give a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. The reason must name the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary, for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable, because it is exophial-specific.
  No entry in the Rust column reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id in that list.
  Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. Each enforced rule prints `path:line: ASPnnn`. Each enforced rule blocks. Each enforced rule has a committed violating fixture and a committed satisfying fixture. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for that rule and exits 0.
  Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced. Examples: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. No rule is report-only; every enforced rule blocks. This is not a Python or TypeScript change.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Prior art: python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304) and rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417).
  Priority P1.
  Decomposed child: Build a blocking gate for Rust source files in the rust/ directory of the Aspergillus repository. Today rust/ holds configs and a README only. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  The gate binary reads Rust source files. For each violation the gate prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The gate exits 1 when a rule fires. The gate exits 0 when no rule fires. The gate blocks. No rule is report-only.
  An enforced rule runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny.
  The gate owns this closed set of single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417. Sibling parts add every rule other than ASP303.
  Establish the committed fixture layout. Each rule id owns one committed violating fixture and one committed satisfying fixture. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for that rule and exits 0. Commit the fixture pair for ASP303.

The gate over the violating fixture prints ASP303 and exits 1. The gate over the satisfying fixture prints no ASP303 line and exits 0.

  The Rust toolchain gates pass in rust/. `cargo test` passes. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes. The `cargo test` suite must be adequate. It must fail when the gate's own logic changes.
  The Python rules file python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py is the prior art for ASP303. This part changes no Python code and no TypeScript code. This part does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling part fixes those.

- c2: The gate's Rust sources under rust/src declare the closed set of 18 single-file rule ids: ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417.
- c3: The repository commits a violating fixture for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs.
- c4: The repository commits a satisfying fixture for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs.

- c6: The gate over rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs prints no ASP303 line and exits 0.

- c8: The Rust column of the ASP303 table row in docs/design.md names `aspergillus-gate` as the enforcing check.

- c11: `cargo clippy -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass in rust/.

- c2: The Rust sources of the new checker, under rust/src, carry the names of the eighteen checks the checker owns. All eighteen names appear there.
- c3: The repository holds the bad example file for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/violating.rs.
- c4: The repository holds the good example file for ASP303 at rust/tests/fixtures/asp303/satisfying.rs.
- c5: A person runs the new Rust checker over the stored bad example for ASP303. At least one reported line names ASP303. The checker finishes with a failure status of 1.
- c6: A person runs the new Rust checker over the stored good example for ASP303. No reported line names ASP303. The checker finishes with a success status of 0.

Each file holds exactly one of the three named mistakes: dropping an error with .ok(), throwing an error away with let _ =, and replacing an error with a default value through unwrap_or_default. The person runs the new Rust checker over each file. The checker names ASP303 for all three files.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo workspace directory. The gate prints each finding in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Every other Rust rule that has a check also has two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` file and a `src/lib.rs` file. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires on a real violation. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate does the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate prints no ASP203 line in any other form. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.

The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds configs and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.

restatement:

The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate does the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds configs and a README. It holds no gate program.   This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate scans a Cargo package directory. The gate prints each finding in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  A Rust rule that has a check also needs two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` file and a `src/lib.rs` file. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires on a real violation. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate does the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate prints no ASP203 line in any other form. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

This is net-new feature work (a new rule), landed feature-shaped: the fixture tests ARE the outer-loop acceptance per aspergillus's own testing.md ("a rule's e2e is the rule firing on real fixture code").

THE INVARIANT. A test file that BOTH (1) constructs a configured system-under-test class in-process AND (2) calls a configured loop-drive method on it is the signature of an in-process e2e — the fake-gate shape a genuine e2e (crossing a real subprocess / installed-CLI / network boundary) is supposed to prevent. exophial's script hardcodes _CONSTRUCT_NAME = "Dispatcher", _DRIVE_ATTRS = {tick, dispatch_ready}, and scans only tests/e2e/. ASP410 lifts the same invariant into the corpus. Same AST-not-text property (exo-8e0): detection is over real cst.Call nodes, so a docstring/comment/string that merely NAMES Dispatcher().tick() is invisible.

CONFIG MECHANISM (the one real design decision). The rule is configurable via three OVERRIDABLE CLASS ATTRIBUTES tuned by subclassing — CONSTRUCT_CLASS_NAMES, DRIVE_METHOD_NAMES, E2E_PATH_PATTERN. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). I did NOT model it on the [tool.aspergillus] extra_io_functions TOML option that the task flagged: verified against source that pebble asp-b72's finding holds — no rule reads that option, it is inert. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

SHAPE. A standard single-file fixit LintRule (no cross-file analysis) as the design discussion concluded. Module-level aggregation: visit_Call accumulates construct nodes and a drive flag, leave_Module reports iff BOTH are present AND the path matches. Detection-only, no autofix (the fix — which real boundary call replaces the in-process construction — is human/agent judgment, same as ASP409); lands at warn per the severity-graduation ADR.

REGISTRATION. Registered in BOTH catalog/__init__.py AND the parent rules/__init__.py re-export. The parent re-export is the load-bearing seam fixit's `enable=["aspergillus.rules"]` walk actually discovers (it does not recurse into the catalog subpackage). A discovery test (test_rule_is_discoverable_by_fixit) asserts collect_rules reaches ASP410.

FOUND BUG (filed, not fixed here) — asp-321. While wiring registration I found ASP409 ShellToSelf is exported from catalog/__init__.py but MISSING from the parent rules/__init__.py re-export, so fixit NEVER discovers it: collect_rules(generate_config(...)) returns 16 rules and ShellToSelf is not among them. ASP409 is defined and unit-tested but never enforced in any consumer's pre-commit path — same inert class as asp-b72. NOT bundled into this pebble: enabling ASP409 repo-wide is a behavior change to a different rule with its own blast radius (may newly flag existing code) that deserves its own verification. Filed as asp-321 (P2) with the one-line fix + the discovery-test pattern to lock it.

Full commands + output in verify_transcript.

  Who is it for? Who uses this and in what situation? Maintainers of Rust repositories adopting Aspergillus (first consumer lobaria).
  How does a person USE the finished thing — what do they SEE and DO? Describe the observable behavior, i.e. how you would demo it. docs/design.md's Rust column names an enforcing check for each of ASP302, ASP303, ASP304, ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409, ASP410, ASP411, ASP412, ASP413, ASP414, ASP415, ASP416 and ASP417, or a one-line reason it does not apply to Rust (for example a rule the Rust type system already enforces, naming the language feature). Each enforced rule runs from the gate binary or a clippy lint the gate forces at deny, prints `path:line: ASPnnn`, blocks, and has a committed violating and satisfying fixture pair. Rules with a direct Rust analogue are enforced, for example: ASP303 an error swallowed into a success value (`.ok()` discarding an Err, `let _ =` on a Result, `unwrap_or_default` on a Result); ASP304 a failure that drops its evidence (`map_err(|_| ..)` discarding the source error); ASP411 match arms with identical bodies; ASP413 a wildcard arm over an enum; ASP414 dispatch on string literals that shadow an enum's variants; ASP416 a function over its input that returns bool or Result<(), E> instead of the parsed type. ASP501 also finds duplicated statement sequences inside otherwise different functions, as the Python check-duplicates CLI does (whole-body + sliding-window + type-1). ASP502 also finds a duplicated type under a different name or with reordered fields (same field names and types). ASP203 has a fixture pair.
  What does 'done' look like in plain language? State the acceptance you could check without reading any code. docs/design.md Rust column: no entry reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported' for any ASP id listed above. For every enforced rule, running the gate over its violating fixture prints that rule id and exits 1, and over its satisfying fixture prints nothing for it and exits 0. ASP502 over a two-crate probe with `struct Lamports(pub u64)` and `struct Balance(pub u64)` reports both; with `struct P{a:i32,b:i32}` and `struct P{b:i32,a:i32}` reports both. ASP501 over a probe with a 6-statement block copied into two otherwise different functions reports both. cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  What are the non-goals / constraints? What must this NOT do? Not ASP202/204/205/206 (a sibling pebble fixes those). No report-only rule: every enforced rule blocks. Not a Python or TypeScript change. ASP415 (exophial reducer reachability) may be stated as not applicable if it is exophial-specific.
  Any examples or references? (links, prior art, a similar thing you like) python/src/aspergillus/rules/level3.py (ASP302-304), rules/catalog/*.py (ASP401-417), python/src/aspergillus/duplicates.py and __main__.py check-duplicates (fragment + type-1 passes). Verification 2026-09-23 (cloud agents VerifyASP202, VerifyASP205_206, VerifySingleFileRules, VerifyDupRules, VerifyLobariaGate; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7): ASP501 is whole-body only and misses copied statement spines; ASP502 misses a renamed duplicate and a field reorder; ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  What priority is this? (P0–P4) and why now? P1
  Decomposed child: Give the Rust ASP203 check a committed violating fixture and a committed satisfying fixture. The audience is maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules; aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no fixture pair.
  Acceptance: ASP203 has a fixture pair. Running the gate over the violating fixture prints `path:line: ASP203` and exits 1. Running the gate over the satisfying fixture prints nothing for ASP203 and exits 0. The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The check blocks.
  Non-goals: this is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. No report-only behavior; the check blocks. This is not a Python or TypeScript change.
  cargo test, cargo clippy -D warnings and cargo fmt --check pass in rust/.
  Priority P1.

criticality: negligible

goal: Commit a violating fixture crate and a satisfying fixture crate for the Rust ASP203 rule, and show that the Aspergillus Rust gate prints `path:line: ASP203` and exits 1 over the violating crate, and prints no ASP203 line and exits 0 over the satisfying crate.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships a Rust gate. The gate reads a Cargo package directory. The gate prints each finding in the form `path:line: ASPnnn`. The rule ASP203 forbids global mutable state. In Rust a `static mut` declaration is global mutable state.
  Each Rust rule that has a check also needs two small committed crates under `rust/fixtures/<rule id>/`. One crate breaks the rule. One crate obeys the rule. Each crate holds a `Cargo.toml` file and a `src/lib.rs` file. The pair is the readable evidence that the check fires on a real violation. The pair is also the evidence that the check stays quiet on clean code. A verification on 2026-09-23 (cloud agent VerifySingleFileRules, aspergillus integrated 019f8b9, lobaria integrated d0269c7) found that ASP203 has no such pair. So no committed evidence shows that the ASP203 check works. A regression in that check stays invisible.
  This request closes that gap. The repository commits a violating fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/`. That crate declares a `static mut`. The repository also commits a satisfying fixture crate at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`. That crate does the same job with no `static mut`. Git tracks the files of both crates. So both crates are committed. They are not untracked working files.
  The acceptance is what a person sees when they run the gate. The person runs the gate over the violating crate. The gate prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`. The gate prints no ASP203 line in any other form. The gate exits with status 1. The person then runs the gate over the satisfying crate. The gate prints no ASP203 line. The gate exits with status 0. The ASP203 finding therefore blocks. The check is not report-only.
  The check runs from the gate binary, or from a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The Rust toolchain checks in `rust/` stay green. `cargo test` passes for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`. Its tests are strong enough to catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code. `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes. `cargo fmt --check` passes.
  The audience is the maintainers of Rust repositories that adopt Aspergillus. The first consumer is lobaria.
  Non-goals. This is not a change to ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206, because a sibling pebble fixes those. This is not a Python change. This is not a TypeScript change. The check must not become report-only.

restatement_clauses:
- c1: A violating fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/Cargo.toml`.
- c2: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/src/lib.rs` declares global mutable state with `static mut`.
- c3: A satisfying fixture crate exists at `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` and carries its own package manifest `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/Cargo.toml`.
- c4: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` exists, so the gate has real Rust code to read in the satisfying crate.
- c5: The file `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/src/lib.rs` declares no `static mut`.
- c6: Git tracks the files of both fixture crates: at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` and at least 2 tracked files under `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/`, so both crates are committed and not untracked working files.
- c7: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/violating/` prints at least one line in the form `path:line: ASP203`, prints no ASP203 line in any other form, and exits with status 1, so the ASP203 finding blocks and is not report-only.
- c8: Running the Aspergillus Rust gate over `rust/fixtures/ASP203/satisfying/` prints no line for ASP203 and exits with status 0.
- c9: `cargo test` passes in `rust/` for the package `aspergillus-rust-gate`, and its tests catch a deliberate break in the changed gate code.
- c10: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` both pass in `rust/`.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: The repository holds the package file of the sample Rust project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule.
- c2: The source file of the sample project that breaks the rule keeps a global value that any code can change.
- c3: The repository holds the package file of the second sample Rust project, the one that follows the global-mutable-state rule.
- c4: The sample Rust project that follows the rule carries a source file, so the checker has real code to read.
- c5: The source file of the sample project that follows the rule keeps no global value that any code can change.
- c6: A report asks the repository which files it keeps for each of the two sample projects. The report says the repository keeps at least two files for the project that breaks the rule. It says the repository keeps at least two files for the project that follows the rule.
- c7: A report runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that breaks the global-mutable-state rule. The report says how many printed lines name the file, then the line number, then ASP203. It says how many ASP203 lines came out in any other form. It says the status the run ended with.
- c8: A report runs the Aspergillus Rust checker over the sample project that follows the global-mutable-state rule. The report says how many ASP203 lines the checker printed. It says the status the run ended with.
- c9: The Rust test suite of the checker passes. It is strong enough that a deliberate break in the changed checker code makes a test fail.
- c10: A report runs the Rust formatting check and the Rust lint check over the repository's Rust code. The report says the status of the formatting check. It says the status of the lint check with every warning treated as an error.

A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.

ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell.   This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

- c12: cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/ and cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.

acceptance_criteria:
- c1: Point the Rust checker at every stored bad example at one time. A report states how many different rule numbers the checker named, how many printed lines did not read as a file path, then a line number, then a rule number, and whether the checker refused the run.
- c2: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example of a chained map, then over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP401 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c3: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example of a chained filter, then over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP402 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c4: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that walks one list several times to add up several totals. Then run it over the stored good example that walks the list one time. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP406 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c5: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that wraps another function and adds nothing. Then run it over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP407 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c6: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that hides a hardcoded answer, or a branch on the environment. Then run it over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP408 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c7: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example that starts its own package in a separate process. Then run it over the stored good example that calls the package directly. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP409 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c8: Run the Rust checker over the stored bad example of a test that builds the system inside itself yet calls itself an end-to-end test. Then run it over the stored good example. A report states whether the checker named rule ASP410 for each file. The report states whether the checker refused each run.
- c9: Open the design document at the part titled 'Rust coverage for ASP4xx'. All eight rule numbers ASP401, ASP402, ASP405, ASP406, ASP407, ASP408, ASP409 and ASP410 appear there. Each one sits on a table row with a filled-in Rust entry beside it.
- c10: Read the same 'Rust coverage for ASP4xx' part of the design document. No entry there puts the work off with the words 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
- c11: The Rust test suite for the checker package runs and passes. The tests also notice when the checker's own logic is altered. They therefore check real behavior, and they do not pass by default.
- c12: Run the Rust linter with warnings treated as errors in the rust/ directory. Also run the Rust formatter in check mode there. A report states the result of each one.

restatement:

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds a configs folder and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.

Same AST-not-text property (exo-8e0): detection is over real cst.Call nodes, so a docstring/comment/string that merely NAMES Dispatcher().tick() is invisible.

CONFIG MECHANISM (the one real design decision). The rule is configurable via three OVERRIDABLE CLASS ATTRIBUTES tuned by subclassing — CONSTRUCT_CLASS_NAMES, DRIVE_METHOD_NAMES, E2E_PATH_PATTERN. This is the idiomatic fixit mechanism aspergillus rules actually honor (cf. MAX_LINES on FunctionTooLong, MIN_ASSERTS on ASP202, own_package on ASP409). I did NOT model it on the [tool.aspergillus] extra_io_functions TOML option that the task flagged: verified against source that pebble asp-b72's finding holds — no rule reads that option, it is inert. The class-attribute-by-subclass pattern is proven working (test_construct_and_drive_names_are_configurable retargets to a "Server"/"serve" SUT and shows the default Dispatcher shape no longer fires under that config). The DEFAULT config reproduces the motivating exophial invariant (Dispatcher + {tick, dispatch_ready}, all paths) so the rule is immediately testable and demonstrable; a consumer retargets for its own SUT. E2E_PATH_PATTERN gates by the file's POSIX path via libcst FilePathProvider metadata (fnmatch glob; default "" = all files — kept empty so the standard VALID/INVALID harness, which runs under invalid.py, works; path-scoping is opt-in and tested separately).

SHAPE. A standard single-file fixit LintRule (no cross-file analysis) as the design discussion concluded. Module-level aggregation: visit_Call accumulates construct nodes and a drive flag, leave_Module reports iff BOTH are present AND the path matches. Detection-only, no autofix (the fix — which real boundary call replaces the in-process construction — is human/agent judgment, same as ASP409); lands at warn per the severity-graduation ADR.

REGISTRATION. Registered in BOTH catalog/__init__.py AND the parent rules/__init__.py re-export. The parent re-export is the load-bearing seam fixit's `enable=["aspergillus.rules"]` walk actually discovers (it does not recurse into the catalog subpackage). A discovery test (test_rule_is_discoverable_by_fixit) asserts collect_rules reaches ASP410.

ASP409 is defined and unit-tested but never enforced in any consumer's pre-commit path — same inert class as asp-b72. NOT bundled into this pebble: enabling ASP409 repo-wide is a behavior change to a different rule with its own blast radius (may newly flag existing code) that deserves its own verification. Filed as asp-321 (P2) with the one-line fix + the discovery-test pattern to lock it.

restatement:
  Aspergillus ships Rust support as configuration only today. The rust/ directory holds a configs folder and a README. It holds no gate program. A maintainer of a Rust repository that adopts Aspergillus therefore gets no enforcement of the ASP4xx catalog rules. The first repository that needs this enforcement is lobaria.
  This request asks for one deliverable. The deliverable is a Rust gate program in rust/, built as the cargo package `aspergillus-gate`. The gate reads Rust source paths. It prints one line of the form `path:line: ASPnnn` for each violation. It exits 1 when at least one rule fires. It exits 0 when no rule fires. A rule runs inside the gate program, or it runs as a clippy lint that the gate forces at deny. The gate reports a clippy-backed rule in the same `path:line: ASPnnn` form. Every enforced rule blocks. No rule is report-only.
  Seven of the eight named ids have a direct Rust analogue. The gate enforces all seven. ASP401 `MapFusion` reports `map(f).map(g)` that should be one composed map. ASP402 `FilterFusion` reports `filter(p).filter(q)` that should be one composed filter. ASP406 `Tupling` reports a multi-pass aggregation over one iterable that should be one pass. ASP407 `WorkerWrapper` reports a trivial pass-through wrapper. ASP408 `AntiSpecialCasing` reports a hardcoded answer, or an environment branch, that games a check. ASP409 `ShellToSelf` reports your own package invoked through a subprocess. ASP410 `InProcessE2E` reports in-process construction of the system under test in a test that calls itself end-to-end.
  The eighth id, ASP405, carries no Python rule. Python leaves ASP405 deliberately unassigned. catalog/__init__.py records the reason. Rust still needs an entry for ASP405. That entry is an enforcing check, or a one-line reason the rule does not apply to Rust. A reason names the language feature that makes the rule unnecessary. An example is a property that the Rust type system already enforces.
  Each enforced rule owns two committed fixtures. The violating fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/violating.rs. The satisfying fixture is at rust/fixtures/aspNNN/satisfying.rs. Over the violating fixture the gate prints that rule id and exits 1. Over the satisfying fixture the gate prints no line for that rule id and exits 0.
  The documentation carries the same map. docs/design.md gains a section named `Rust coverage for ASP4xx`. Inside that section each of the eight ids appears as a markdown table row that starts `| ASPnnn |` and carries a non-empty Rust entry in the next cell. The entry names an enforcing check, or gives the one-line reason. No entry for those ids reads 'Python only', 'Manual', 'planned' or 'not yet ported'.
  The Rust toolchain stays green. cargo test passes in rust/ for the `aspergillus-gate` package. The tests catch a change to the gate code they cover. cargo clippy -D warnings passes in rust/. cargo fmt --check passes in rust/.
  This work does not change ASP202, ASP204, ASP205 or ASP206. A sibling pebble fixes those. This work does not change the Python surface. This work does not change the TypeScript surface.
